entries.title: Open a notebook in Colab
entries.summary: Three ways in: from Google Drive, by uploading the `.ipynb` file, or through the Open in Colab badge at the top of each course notebook.
entries.syntax:
Drive:   right-click the .ipynb → Open with → Google Colaboratory
Upload:  colab.research.google.com → File ▸ Upload notebook
Badge:   click “Open in Colab” at the top of the notebook (opens it from GitHub)
entries.gotcha: A notebook opened from GitHub is read-only. Save your own copy (File ▸ Save a copy in Drive) before editing, or your work disappears when the tab closes.

entries.title: Run a cell: Shift+Enter
entries.summary: A notebook is a stack of cells. Run one and its output appears right underneath; run the Setup cell first, then work top to bottom.
entries.syntax:
Shift+Enter          run the cell, move to the next one
Ctrl/Cmd+Enter       run the cell, stay on it
▶ (left of the cell)  same as Ctrl/Cmd+Enter
Runtime ▸ Run all    run every cell from the top
entries.gotcha: All cells share one memory. Skipping a cell is the usual cause of `NameError: name 'pd' is not defined`: the import cell above it never ran.

entries.title: Code cells vs text cells
entries.summary: Colab has two kinds of cell: code cells run Python (or shell lines starting with `!`), text cells hold Markdown for notes, headings and links.
entries.syntax:
+ Code   → a cell that runs Python
+ Text   → a cell of Markdown
Cmd/Ctrl+M M   convert code → text     Cmd/Ctrl+M Y   convert text → code
entries.gotcha: Markdown typed into a code cell is a syntax error, and Python typed into a text cell is just text. If a cell looks wrong, check which kind it is.

entries.title: Colab keyboard shortcuts
entries.summary: The five shortcuts used in class, plus where to find the rest.
entries.syntax:
A               new cell above
B               new cell below
Cmd/Ctrl+M D    delete the cell
Cmd/Ctrl+M M    turn a code cell into a text cell
Cmd/Ctrl+M Y    turn a text cell into a code cell
Tools ▸ Keyboard shortcuts    the full list
entries.gotcha: The letter shortcuts work when the cell is selected but you are not typing inside it: press Esc first, then the shortcut.

entries.title: Jupyter keyboard shortcuts (local notebooks)
entries.summary: Jupyter uses the same idea with shorter keys: leave the cell with Esc, then one letter does the job.
entries.syntax:
Esc      leave the cell (command mode)
D, D     delete the cell (press D twice)
M        turn the cell into Markdown
Y        turn the cell into code
Enter    go back to typing inside the cell
entries.gotcha: In Jupyter you press D twice to delete; in Colab it is Cmd/Ctrl+M and then D.

entries.title: Save a copy in Drive
entries.summary: Makes the notebook yours: edits, notes and experiments are kept in your Google Drive.
entries.syntax: File ▸ Save a copy in Drive
entries.gotcha: The copy lands in a Drive folder called “Colab Notebooks” with “Copy of” in its name. Rename it (click the title) so you can find it next week.

entries.title: Stop a runaway cell
entries.summary: When a cell keeps spinning, interrupt it, find what never changed, and run it again.
entries.syntax:
click the cell's ■ stop button
Runtime ▸ Interrupt execution
entries.gotcha: A cell that never finishes is usually a `while` loop whose condition never becomes `False`. Every programmer has done this; the skill is spotting the spin quickly.

entries.title: Files written by your code: the Files panel
entries.summary: Files that your code saves (`notes.txt`, `record.json`, a figure) appear in the Files panel on the left, where you can download them.
entries.syntax: left sidebar → folder icon (Files) → hover a file → ⋮ → Download
entries.gotcha: Those files live on the Colab machine, not in Drive, and vanish when the runtime ends. Download anything you want to keep.

entries.title: print() — show a value
entries.summary: Writes one or more values to the screen, separated by spaces, followed by a new line.
entries.syntax:
print(value)
print(value1, value2, ...)
print(value, end=" ")      # stay on the same line
entries.example:
print("Hello, world!")

total = 3 + 4
print("The total is", total)

for n in range(3):
    print(n, end=" ")       # no new line after each one
print()
entries.gotcha: Text must be in quotes. `print(Hello)` without quotes raises `NameError: name 'Hello' is not defined`.

entries.title: Comments with #
entries.summary: Everything after a `#` on a line is ignored by Python. Use comments to say why a key line exists; your future self will thank you.
entries.syntax:
# a comment on its own line
code   # a comment after code
entries.example:
# AI use: none — original draft
# Compute the mean of three quiz scores
scores = [88, 92, 79]
mean = sum(scores) / len(scores)   # divide the total by the count
print(mean)
entries.gotcha: The course AI policy asks for a short comment block at the top of every submission naming any AI tool you used and what you used it for.

entries.title: Assign a variable with =
entries.summary: A variable is a name that refers to a value. The single `=` stores the value on the right under the name on the left.
entries.syntax: name = value
entries.example:
x = 5                  # a number
name = "John"          # text, in quotes
print(x)
print(name)

x = x + 1              # the right side is computed first, then stored
print(x)
entries.gotcha: `=` assigns, `==` compares. `x = 5` is a statement that stores 5; `x == 5` is a question that answers `True` or `False`.

entries.title: Assign several names at once
entries.summary: Chain `=` to give several names the same value, or list names and values with commas to unpack them in one line.
entries.example:
x = y = z = 5          # all three get 5
print(x, y, z)

a, b = 3, 4            # unpacking: a=3, b=4
print(a, b)
entries.gotcha: The number of names must match the number of values: `a, b = 1, 2, 3` raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`.

entries.title: Variable naming rules
entries.summary: Names start with a letter or underscore, continue with letters, digits or underscores, and cannot be a reserved word. Make them meaningful.
entries.syntax:
valid:    my_wealth   _aws_instance   score2   GPA_mean
invalid:  3rd_instance (digit first)   aws-instance (hyphen)   return (reserved word)
entries.example:
my_wealth = 1_000_000       # letters, digits and underscores
_aws_instance = "ok"        # may start with an underscore
print(my_wealth, _aws_instance)

# each of these is a SyntaxError if you uncomment it:
# 3rd_instance = 1          # cannot start with a digit
# aws-instance = 1          # a hyphen is a minus sign
# return = 3                # reserved keyword
entries.gotcha: Names are case-sensitive: `GPA` and `gpa` are two different variables.

entries.title: Arithmetic: + − * / **
entries.summary: Python does math the way a calculator does; an expression is computed and its result can be printed or stored.
entries.syntax: a + b    a - b    a * b    a / b    a ** 2
entries.example:
a, b = 3, 4
print(a + b)      # addition
print(a - b)      # subtraction
print(a * b)      # multiplication
print(a / b)      # division: always gives a decimal (float)
print(a ** 2)     # exponent: a squared

John_GPA, Jane_GPA = 3.15, 3.85
print((John_GPA + Jane_GPA) / 2)
entries.gotcha: `/` always returns a float, even when it divides evenly: `8 / 4` is `2.0`. Week 3 adds `//` (whole-number division) and `%` (remainder).

entries.title: Readable numbers: 1_000_000
entries.summary: An underscore inside a number is ignored by Python, so you can write thousands separators for your own eyes.
entries.example:
my_wealth = 1_000_000
print(my_wealth)
print(my_wealth * 2)
entries.gotcha: Only inside a number: `1,000,000` with commas makes a tuple of three numbers, not one million.

entries.title: type() — what kind of value is this?
entries.summary: Reports the data type of any value; the first thing to check when something behaves unexpectedly.
entries.syntax: type(value)
entries.example:
age = 16
age_text = "16"
print(type(age))
print(type(age_text))
print(type(3.14))
print(type(True))
print(type({"cat": "persian"}))
entries.gotcha: `"16"` and `16` look alike but have different types, so `"16" + 1` fails. Convert first with `int("16")`.

entries.title: del — remove a variable
entries.summary: Deletes the name; using it afterwards raises `NameError`.
entries.syntax: del name
entries.example:
model = "gbt"
print(model)
del model
print(model)        # the name no longer exists
entries.output:
gbt
NameError: name 'model' is not defined
entries.gotcha: You rarely need `del` in a notebook. Re-running the cell that defines a variable recreates it.

entries.title: Text needs quotes: "16" is not 16
entries.summary: Quotes (single or double) tell Python a value is text. Text that looks like a number is still text, and `+` joins text instead of adding.
entries.syntax:
name = "John"
name = 'John'      # single quotes work the same way
entries.example:
age = 16           # a number
age_text = "16"    # text that happens to look like a number
print(age + 1)
print(age_text + "1")        # + joins two strings
print(type(age), type(age_text))
entries.gotcha: Mixing the two raises `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`. Convert with `int(age_text)` or `str(age)` first.

entries.title: The interactive interpreter (REPL)
entries.summary: Typing `python` in a terminal starts a prompt where each line runs immediately, like a single notebook cell at a time.
entries.syntax:
$ conda activate hudm5001
$ python
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> exit()          # or Ctrl+D
entries.gotcha: The `>>>` is the prompt, not something you type. To run a whole file instead, use `python script.py`.

entries.title: A minimal script with the __main__ guard
entries.summary: A `.py` file that defines a function and, when run directly, calls it. The guard line lets the same file be imported elsewhere without running the demo.
entries.setup:
%%writefile hello.py
# hello.py
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":      # runs only when executed directly
    print(greet("HUDM 5001"))
entries.setup_note: write the file hello.py (a %%writefile cell in Colab, or any editor locally)
entries.example: !python hello.py
entries.gotcha: Inside Colab the `!` sends the command to the shell; in a terminal you type `python hello.py` without it.

entries.title: Check that the course packages import
entries.summary: One cell that imports the main libraries and prints their versions; if it runs without an error, the setup is complete.
entries.syntax:
import sys, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, plotly
print(sys.version.split()[0], numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)
entries.example:
import sys, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, plotly
print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
print("numpy", numpy.__version__, "| pandas", pandas.__version__)
entries.output_note: The numbers you see depend on when you installed. Colab today reports Python 3.13 and pandas 2.2.
entries.gotcha: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'plotly'` means the package is missing from the active environment: `conda install -c conda-forge plotly` (or `python -m pip install plotly`) and try again. If it is installed but still missing, `python -m pip --version` shows which Python your pip serves; it must be the same environment.

entries.title: Booleans: True and False
entries.summary: A boolean is either `True` or `False`. Every comparison produces one, and every decision in your code runs on them.
entries.syntax:
flag = True
flag = False
result = 3 > 2      # a comparison gives a bool
entries.example:
exam_pass = True
print(exam_pass)
print(type(exam_pass))
print(3 > 2)          # comparisons produce booleans
print(3 == 2)
entries.gotcha: Capital letters matter: `true` and `false` are not defined; only `True` and `False` are.

entries.title: isinstance() — is this value of that type?
entries.summary: Answers `True` or `False` for “is this value an int / float / str / …?”, which is handier than `type()` inside a condition.
entries.syntax: isinstance(value, type)
entries.example:
epoch = 21
pi = 3.1415926
print(isinstance(epoch, int))
print(isinstance(pi, float))
print(isinstance(pi, int))
print(isinstance("21", str))
entries.gotcha: `isinstance(True, int)` is `True`, because Python treats booleans as a special kind of integer (`True` counts as 1).

entries.title: and, or, not — combine conditions
entries.summary: `and` needs both sides true, `or` needs at least one, `not` flips. Python short-circuits: once the left side decides, the right side is never looked at.
entries.syntax:
A and B
A or B
not A
entries.example:
exam_pass = True
graduation = False
print(exam_pass and graduation)
print(exam_pass or graduation)
print(not exam_pass)

# short-circuit: the right side never runs, so 1/0 raises no error
print(False and (1 / 0 > 0))
entries.gotcha: These words work on single `True`/`False` values. For whole pandas columns you need `&` and `|` instead (week 4).

entries.title: int and float — whole numbers and decimals
entries.summary: `int` is a whole number (21, -4); `float` has a decimal point (0.95, 3.14). Division always produces a float.
entries.syntax:
epoch = 21        # int
pi = 3.14         # float
entries.example:
epoch = 21
pi = 3.1415926
print(epoch, type(epoch))
print(pi, type(pi))
print(7 / 2)          # division always gives a float
print(7.0 + 1)        # mixing int and float gives a float
print(0.1 + 0.2)      # floats are approximate
entries.gotcha: Floats are rounded in binary, so `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`. Use `round()` when you display them.

entries.title: round(x, ndigits)
entries.summary: Rounds a number to a given number of decimal places; with no second argument it rounds to a whole number.
entries.syntax:
round(number, ndigits)
round(number)
entries.example:
pi = 3.1415926
print(round(pi, 2))
print(round(pi))
print(round(66.49000000000001, 2))   # tidy a floating-point result
entries.gotcha: `round(2.5)` gives `2`, not `3`: Python rounds a half to the even neighbour. For display, an f-string spec `f"{x:.2f}"` is often what you want.

entries.title: String indexing and slicing
entries.summary: Characters are numbered from 0. `s[i]` picks one, `s[start:stop]` picks a range where `stop` is excluded, and negative numbers count from the end.
entries.syntax:
s[0]        # first character
s[-1]       # last character
s[:2]       # first two
s[-2:]      # last two
s[2:5]      # positions 2, 3, 4
entries.example:
status = "success"
print(status[0])        # first character
print(status[-1])       # last character
print(status[:2])       # first two
print(status[-2:])      # last two
print(status[2:5])      # positions 2, 3, 4 (5 is left out)
entries.gotcha: The stop position is not included: `status[2:5]` gives three characters, not four. Asking for a position that does not exist raises `IndexError`.

entries.title: len() — how many items
entries.summary: Counts the characters in a string or the items in a list, tuple, set or dict.
entries.syntax: len(value)
entries.example:
print(len("success"))
print(len(["futures", "swaps", "options"]))
print(len({"Arizona": "Phoenix", "Colorado": "Denver"}))
print(len("May the force be with you.".split()))   # word count
entries.gotcha: `len(150)` fails with `TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()`. Numbers have no length; convert to text first if you want the number of digits.

entries.title: String methods: upper, lower, strip, startswith, endswith
entries.summary: Methods are attached to the value with a dot. These five change case, trim whitespace, or test how the text begins or ends.
entries.syntax:
s.upper()
s.lower()
s.strip()
s.startswith("a")
s.endswith("s")
entries.example:
status = "success"
print(status.upper())
print("SUCCESS".lower())
print("  trim me  ".strip())
print(status.startswith("a"))
print(status.endswith("s"))
print(status.upper().lower())     # methods can be chained
entries.output:
SUCCESS
success
trim me
False
True
success
entries.gotcha: The parentheses are required: `status.upper` without them is the method itself, not the uppercased text.

entries.title: str.replace() — swap one piece of text for another
entries.summary: Returns a new string with every occurrence of the first text replaced by the second; the original is untouched.
entries.syntax: s.replace(old, new)
entries.example:
status = "success"
print(status.replace("s", "y"))
print(status)                       # the original is unchanged

text = "the model is fast and the model is accurate"
print(text.replace(" is ", " "))    # drop a stop word everywhere
entries.output:
yucceyy
success
the model fast and the model accurate
entries.gotcha: Replacing `"is"` also hits the inside of words such as `"this"`. Pad with spaces (`" is "`) to match whole words, the trick from Exercise 4.

entries.title: str.split() — text into a list of words
entries.summary: Cuts a string into a list, at whitespace by default or at any separator you name.
entries.syntax:
s.split()          # at spaces, tabs, newlines
s.split(",")       # at a comma
entries.example:
got = "You know nothing, Jon Snow."
print(got.split())            # on whitespace
print(got.split(","))         # on a comma
print(len(got.split()))       # word count
entries.gotcha: Punctuation stays attached: `"nothing,"` keeps its comma. Lowercase and `.replace()` the punctuation away first if you are counting words.

entries.title: Strings are immutable
entries.summary: You cannot change one character of a string in place; you can only build a new string and reassign the name.
entries.syntax:
s = "Xuccess"      # fine: a new string
s[0] = "X"         # TypeError
entries.example:
status = "success"
status = "Xuccess"        # reassigning the whole variable is fine
print(status)
status[0] = "s"           # editing one character in place is not
entries.output:
Xuccess
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
entries.gotcha: This is why string methods such as `.replace()` and `.upper()` return a new value: assign the result to a name or it is lost.

entries.title: Join strings with +
entries.summary: `+` glues two strings end to end, useful for building paths and messages.
entries.syntax: "text" + variable + "more text"
entries.example:
root_path = "/Users/ys2952/repo/hudm5001/"
file = "iris.csv"
print(root_path + file)

long_str, name = "You know nothing, ", "Jon Snow."
print(long_str + name)
entries.gotcha: Both sides must be strings: `"Age: " + 16` fails. Write `"Age: " + str(16)`, or better, an f-string.

entries.title: f-strings and .format()
entries.summary: Insert values into text by writing the variable inside `{}` in a string that starts with `f`; `.format()` is the older equivalent.
entries.syntax:
f"text {variable} text"
f"{value:.2f}"                    # format spec: 2 decimals
"text {} text".format(variable)
entries.example:
epoch, loss = 3, 0.12345
print(f"Epoch: {epoch}, loss: {loss}")
print("Epoch: {}, loss: {}".format(epoch, loss))

# a format spec after a colon controls the look
print(f"loss rounded: {loss:.2f}")
print(f"{'name':10s}|{'score':>6}")     # pad to a width
entries.output:
Epoch: 3, loss: 0.12345
Epoch: 3, loss: 0.12345
loss rounded: 0.12
name      | score
entries.gotcha: Forget the `f` and the braces are printed literally: `"{epoch}"` stays `{epoch}`.

entries.title: Lists: create, index, slice
entries.summary: A list is an ordered collection in square brackets. It can hold mixed types and is indexed and sliced exactly like a string.
entries.syntax:
items = ["a", "b", "c"]
items[0]      items[-1]      items[:2]
entries.example:
financial_derivatives = ["futures", "swaps", "options"]
print(type(financial_derivatives))
print(financial_derivatives[0])          # first item
print(financial_derivatives[-1])         # last item
print(financial_derivatives[:2])         # first two
print(financial_derivatives[0][:3])      # first 3 characters of the first item

mixed = ["a", 5, 3.2]                    # mixed types are fine
print(len(mixed))
entries.gotcha: Indexing starts at 0, so `items[3]` on a three-item list raises `IndexError: list index out of range`.

entries.title: Change a list: item assignment, append, remove, +
entries.summary: Lists are mutable: replace an item by position, add to the end with `.append()`, drop the first match with `.remove()`, and join two lists with `+`.
entries.syntax:
items[1] = "new"
items.append("x")
items.remove("x")
items + other_items
entries.example:
derivatives = ["futures", "swaps", "options"]
derivatives[1] = "forwards"          # change an item
derivatives.append("bonds")          # add to the end
print(derivatives)

derivatives.remove("futures")        # remove the first match
print(derivatives)

print(["x1", "x2"] + ["x3", "x4"])   # + joins two lists
entries.gotcha: `.append()` and `.remove()` change the list and return `None`, so `new = items.append("x")` leaves `new` empty. `.remove()` only takes out the first occurrence.

entries.title: list.sort() and sorted()
entries.summary: `.sort()` reorders the list in place, smallest first (`reverse=True` for largest first); `sorted()` returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone.
entries.syntax:
items.sort()
items.sort(reverse=True)
sorted(items)
entries.example:
num_list = [5, 2, 7, 4, 9]
num_list.sort()
print(num_list)
num_list.sort(reverse=True)
print(num_list)

names = ["John", "Zack", "Jack", "Alice"]
names.sort()                     # alphabetical
print(names)

print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))         # a new list; the original is unchanged
entries.gotcha: `x = num_list.sort()` sets `x` to `None`. Sort first, then use the list; or use `sorted()` when you want the result as a value.

entries.title: Nested lists: a list of lists
entries.summary: A list can hold other lists, which is how a grid (an image, a table) is stored; index twice to reach a cell: row first, then column.
entries.syntax:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
grid[0]        # the first row
grid[0][1]     # row 0, column 1
entries.example:
image = [
    [10, 200, 90],
    [255, 128, 0],
    [60, 75, 240],
]
print(image[0])          # the whole first row
print(image[0][0])       # row 0, column 0
print(image[2][:2])      # first two values of the last row

image[0][0] = 0          # lists are mutable, even inside lists
print(image[0])
print(len(image), "rows x", len(image[0]), "columns")
entries.gotcha: `image[0, 0]` with a comma is a NumPy habit that fails on plain lists; use `image[0][0]`.

entries.title: Tuples: ordered and frozen
entries.summary: A tuple is an ordered collection that cannot be changed, written with parentheses (or just commas). Use it for fixed groupings.
entries.syntax:
coffees = ("brazilian", "costa_rican", "colombian")
grab_bag = 4, "EHR", [1, 2]      # commas make the tuple
entries.example:
coffees = ("brazilian", "costa_rican", "colombian")
print(type(coffees))
print(coffees[0])
print(coffees[-2:])

grab_bag = 4, "EHR", ["year", "in", "review"]
print(grab_bag)
print(len(grab_bag))
entries.gotcha: `coffees[0] = "kenyan"` raises `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment`. Functions that return several values hand them back as a tuple.

entries.title: Unpack a tuple into variables
entries.summary: List as many names as there are items and each name receives one item; the same move powers `a, b = 3, 4`, swapping, and `for key, value in ...`.
entries.syntax:
name, age, height = record
a, b = b, a       # swap
entries.example:
record = ("Alice", "29", "1.68")
name, age_text, height_text = record
print(name)
print(int(age_text) + 1)

a, b = 3, 4
a, b = b, a              # swap in one line
print(a, b)
entries.gotcha: The counts must match: unpacking three items into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`.

entries.title: Sets: unique and unordered
entries.summary: A set in curly braces keeps each value once and has no order; it is the tool for de-duplicating and for fast `in` tests.
entries.example:
peanuts = {"snoopy", "snoopy", "woodstock"}
print(peanuts)                  # the duplicate is gone
print("snoopy" in peanuts)
print(len(peanuts))
print(type({}))                 # careful: {} is an empty dict
print(type(set()))
entries.output_note: Sets have no order, so the two names may print in either order on your machine.
entries.gotcha: `peanuts[0]` fails: a set has no positions. Convert with `sorted(peanuts)` when you need an ordered list.

entries.title: set.union() and set.intersection()
entries.summary: Union collects everything in either set; intersection keeps only what is in both.
entries.syntax:
set1.union(set2)
set1.intersection(set2)
entries.output_note: The items inside each set may print in a different order on your machine.
entries.gotcha: `set1 + set2` is a `TypeError`; sets combine with `.union()` (or `|`), not with `+`.

entries.title: set(list) — de-duplicate a list
entries.summary: Wrapping a list in `set()` drops the repeats; `len()` of the result is the number of distinct values.
entries.syntax:
set(items)
len(set(items))
sorted(set(items))     # back to an ordered list
entries.example:
user_a_likes = ["Inception", "Matrix", "Inception", "Interstellar"]
unique = set(user_a_likes)
print(len(user_a_likes), "likes,", len(unique), "distinct")
print(sorted(unique))          # sorted() turns it back into an ordered list
entries.gotcha: The conversion forgets the original order. If order matters, keep the list and use the set only for counting or membership.

entries.title: Dictionaries: key → value
entries.summary: A dict maps keys to values in `{key: value}` pairs. Look up by key in square brackets, and assign to a key to add or change a pair.
entries.example:
state_capital = {"Arizona": "Phoenix", "Colorado": "Denver", "New York": "Albany"}
print(state_capital["New York"])          # look up by key

state_capital["Texas"] = "Austin"         # add a pair
state_capital["Arizona"] = "PHOENIX"      # change a value
print(state_capital)
print(len(state_capital))
entries.gotcha: Looking up a key that is not there raises `KeyError`. Keys are usually strings; values can be anything, including lists and other dicts.

entries.title: .keys(), .values(), .items()
entries.summary: Three views of a dict: all the keys, all the values, or the (key, value) pairs together.
entries.syntax:
d.keys()
d.values()
d.items()
list(d.keys())     # as a plain list
entries.example:
state_capital = {"Arizona": "Phoenix", "Colorado": "Denver", "New York": "Albany"}
print(state_capital.keys())
print(state_capital.values())
print(state_capital.items())
print(list(state_capital.keys()))     # list() turns the view into a plain list
entries.output:
dict_keys(['Arizona', 'Colorado', 'New York'])
dict_values(['Phoenix', 'Denver', 'Albany'])
dict_items([('Arizona', 'Phoenix'), ('Colorado', 'Denver'), ('New York', 'Albany')])
['Arizona', 'Colorado', 'New York']
entries.gotcha: The views are not lists: `d.keys()[0]` fails. Wrap in `list()` first, or loop over them directly.

entries.title: dict.get() — a lookup that never crashes
entries.summary: `.get(key)` returns the value, or `None` (or a default you choose) when the key is missing, where square brackets would raise `KeyError`.
entries.syntax:
d.get(key)
d.get(key, default)
entries.example:
airports = {"LAGUARDIA": "LGA", "LOGAN": "BOS"}
print(airports.get("LOGAN"))
print(airports.get("KENNEDY"))               # missing -> None, no error
print(airports.get("KENNEDY", "unknown"))    # or a default of your choice
print(airports["KENNEDY"])                   # square brackets raise KeyError
entries.gotcha: A silent `None` can hide a typo in the key. Use `.get()` when a missing key is expected, square brackets when it would be a bug.

entries.title: Nested dictionaries
entries.summary: A value can itself be a dict, giving a two-level record such as name → details. Index twice to reach the inner value.
entries.syntax:
profile = {"Jane": {"age": 22, "major": "Learning Analytics"}}
profile["Jane"]["major"]
entries.example:
cryptos = {
    "Bitcoin":  {"abbr": "BTC", "born": 2009, "highest_price": 126_198},
    "Ethereum": {"abbr": "ETH", "born": 2015, "highest_price": 4_946},
}
print(cryptos["Bitcoin"]["abbr"])
ratio = cryptos["Bitcoin"]["highest_price"] / cryptos["Ethereum"]["highest_price"]
print(round(ratio, 1))
print(list(cryptos.keys()))
entries.gotcha: Each level needs its own brackets; `cryptos["Bitcoin", "abbr"]` with a comma looks for one key that is a tuple.

entries.title: range(start, stop, step)
entries.summary: Generates a sequence of integers from `start` up to but not including `stop`; wrap it in `list()` to see the numbers.
entries.syntax:
range(stop)
range(start, stop)
range(start, stop, step)
list(range(...))
entries.example:
num_seq = range(1, 10, 2)
print(num_seq)              # a range object, not a list
print(list(num_seq))
print(list(range(5)))       # start defaults to 0; stop is excluded
print(list(range(10, 0, -3)))
entries.gotcha: `stop` is excluded: `range(1, 10)` ends at 9. Its real job is driving loops: `for i in range(5):` (week 6).

entries.title: int(), float(), str(), list() — convert between types
entries.summary: Call the type's name as a function to convert a value; some conversions need two steps, and some are impossible.
entries.example:
print(int(3.8))            # chops the decimals
print(float("3.8"))        # text -> float
print(str(3.8) + "!")      # number -> text
print(int(float("3.8")))   # two steps for a decimal written as text
print(list(range(3)))
print(int("3.8"))          # a decimal string cannot go straight to int
entries.output:
3
3.8
3.8!
3
[0, 1, 2]
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.8'
entries.gotcha: `int()` truncates toward zero rather than rounding: `int(3.8)` is `3`. Use `round()` when you want the nearest whole number.

entries.title: Mutable vs immutable types
entries.summary: Lists, sets and dicts can be changed in place; numbers, strings and tuples cannot. It matters because two names can point at the same mutable object.
entries.syntax:
mutable:    list   set   dict
immutable:  int    float   bool   str   tuple
entries.example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
alias = nums              # a second name for the SAME list
alias.append(4)
print(nums)               # changed through the other name

word = "abc"
upper = word.upper()      # strings cannot change; methods return new ones
print(word, upper)
entries.gotcha: To copy a list rather than alias it, write `copy = nums.copy()` (or `list(nums)`). The same trap appears with DataFrames, hence `df.copy()` in week 5.

entries.title: sum(), min(), max() on a list
entries.summary: Three built-in functions that summarize a list of numbers; with `len()` they give the mean by hand.
entries.syntax:
sum(items)
min(items)
max(items)
entries.example:
scores = [88, 92, 79]
print(sum(scores))
print(min(scores), max(scores))
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))     # the mean, by hand
entries.gotcha: `sum()` works on numbers, not on strings: `sum(["a", "b"])` is a `TypeError`. Naming a variable `sum` hides the function; call it `total` instead.

entries.title: Floor division //
entries.summary: Divides and rounds down to a whole number; the everyday tool for “how many whole hours are in 137 minutes?”
entries.syntax: a // b
entries.example:
print(5 / 2)       # true division -> 2.5
print(5 // 2)      # floor division -> 2
print(-5 // 2)     # rounds DOWN, toward negative infinity -> -3

minutes = 137
print(minutes // 60, "hours")
entries.gotcha: It rounds toward negative infinity, so `-5 // 2` is `-3`, not `-2`.

entries.title: Modulus % — the remainder
entries.summary: Gives what is left after whole-number division; `x % 2 == 0` is the standard test for an even number.
entries.syntax: a % b
entries.example:
print(5 % 2)              # remainder 1
print(137 % 60, "minutes left over")

n = 339
print("Even?", n % 2 == 0)
print("Odd? ", n % 2 == 1)

# print a progress line every 10th step
for step in range(1, 31):
    if step % 10 == 0:
        print("step", step)
entries.output:
1
17 minutes left over
Even? False
Odd?  True
step 10
step 20
step 30
entries.gotcha: `x % 10 == 0` means “divisible by 10”. Beginners write `x / 10 == 0`, which asks whether x is zero.

entries.title: Exponent **
entries.summary: Raises a number to a power; a fractional power takes a root.
entries.syntax: a ** b
entries.example:
print(5 ** 3)          # 5 cubed
print(2 ** 10)
print(9 ** 0.5)        # square root
print(1.05 ** 3)       # 5% growth for three years
entries.gotcha: `^` is not “to the power of” in Python; it is a bitwise operator that gives surprising numbers. Always use `**`.

entries.title: Comparisons: == != < <= > >=
entries.summary: Each comparison produces a boolean. `==` asks whether two values are equal, `!=` whether they differ.
entries.syntax: a == b    a != b    a < b    a <= b    a > b    a >= b
entries.example:
x = 10
print(0 == (10 % 5))
print(5 / 9 != 0.5555)
print(x >= 10, x > 10)
print("apple" < "banana")     # strings compare alphabetically

score, attendance = 72, 0.9
print("Passed?", (score >= 60) and (attendance >= 0.8))
entries.output:
True
True
True False
True
Passed? True
entries.gotcha: One `=` assigns, two `==` compare. `if score = 60:` is a `SyntaxError`.

entries.title: is vs == (identity vs equality)
entries.summary: `==` asks “same value?”; `is` asks “the very same object in memory?”. Two separate lists with equal contents are `==` but not `is`.
entries.syntax:
a == b       # same value
a is b       # same object
a is not b
entries.example:
x = ["python", "R"]
y = ["python", "R"]     # same contents, a different object
z = x                   # another name for the same object
print(x == y)           # True  -> equal values
print(x is y)           # False -> not the same object
print(x is z)           # True  -> z is x
print(id(x) == id(z))   # id() shows the object's address
entries.gotcha: Use `is` only for `None` (`if r is None:`). For numbers, strings and lists, always compare with `==`.

entries.title: in / not in — membership
entries.summary: Tests whether a value is inside a list, string, set or the keys of a dict.
entries.syntax:
value in collection
value not in collection
entries.example:
print("fries" in ["fries", "burger"])
print("chicken" not in ["fries", "burger"])
print("know" in "You know nothing")        # substring test

grades = {"Ann": 90, "Bob": 85}
print("Ann" in grades)      # dict membership tests the KEYS
print(90 in grades)         # ...not the values
print(90 in grades.values())
entries.output:
True
True
True
True
False
True
entries.gotcha: `in` on a dict looks at keys only. To test a value, use `in d.values()`.

entries.title: Write a text file: with open(path, "w")
entries.summary: Opens a file for writing, hands it to a variable inside the `with` block, and closes it automatically when the block ends.
entries.syntax:
with open("file.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("line 1\n")
entries.example:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("line 1: hello\n")
    file.write("line 2: programming for data science\n")

print(open("notes.txt").read())      # quick check
entries.output:
line 1: hello
line 2: programming for data science
entries.gotcha: `"w"` overwrites the file if it already exists. `.write()` does not add a newline; put `\n` at the end of each line yourself.

entries.title: Read a text file: .read() and .readlines()
entries.summary: Opens a file for reading and pulls its contents into a string (`.read()`) or a list of lines (`.readlines()`).
entries.syntax:
with open("file.txt", "r") as file:
    contents = file.read()
    lines = file.readlines()
entries.setup:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("line 1: hello\nline 2: programming for data science\n")
entries.example:
with open("notes.txt", "r") as file:
    contents = file.read()
print(contents)

with open("notes.txt") as file:        # "r" is the default mode
    lines = file.readlines()
print(len(lines), "lines")
print(lines[0].strip())
entries.output:
line 1: hello
line 2: programming for data science

2 lines
line 1: hello
entries.gotcha: Each line from `.readlines()` keeps its `\n`; call `.strip()` to remove it. Reading a file that does not exist raises `FileNotFoundError`.

entries.title: File modes: "r", "w", "a" and encoding
entries.summary: The second argument to `open()` says what you intend: read, write (overwrite), or append. Add `encoding="utf-8"` for text with accents or emoji.
entries.syntax:
open(path, "r")                     # read (default)
open(path, "w")                     # write: create or overwrite
open(path, "a")                     # append to the end
open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8")
entries.example:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("first run\n")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:           # append keeps what is there
    f.write("second run 🎉\n")
with open("log.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())
entries.gotcha: Opening with `"w"` wipes the file before you write a single character. When in doubt, use `"a"`.

entries.title: json.dump() and json.load()
entries.summary: JSON is text that maps directly onto Python dicts and lists. `json.dump` writes an object to a file, `json.load` reads it back as a normal dict.
entries.syntax:
import json
with open("file.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(obj, f)
with open("file.json") as f:
    obj = json.load(f)
entries.example:
import json

record = {"name": "iris study", "n": 150, "features": ["sepal", "petal"]}

with open("record.json", "w") as file:
    json.dump(record, file)

with open("record.json", "r") as file:
    back = json.load(file)

print(back)
print(back["features"])          # back is a normal dict
print(open("record.json").read())   # what the file itself looks like
entries.gotcha: `json.dumps` / `json.loads` (with an s) work on strings instead of files. Mixing them up gives `TypeError` messages about `write`.

entries.title: JSON refuses NumPy numbers: wrap in int() / float()
entries.summary: Statistics from NumPy or pandas come back as NumPy numbers (`int64`, `float64`), which `json.dump` cannot write. Convert them with `int()` or `float()` first.
entries.syntax: json.dump({"n": int(df.shape[0]), "mean": float(df["x"].mean())}, f)
entries.example:
import json
import numpy as np

total = np.array([1, 2, 3]).sum()
print(type(total))
print(json.dumps({"total": int(total)}))    # wrap it and JSON is happy
print(json.dumps({"total": total}))         # the bare NumPy number fails
entries.output:
<class 'numpy.int64'>
{"total": 6}
TypeError: Object of type int64 is not JSON serializable
entries.gotcha: The error appears only when you save, long after the number was computed. If a summary dict will be written to JSON, convert as you build it.

entries.title: os.getcwd() and os.path — work with paths
entries.summary: The `os` module reports where you are and takes paths apart or builds them in a way that works on Mac, Windows and Linux.
entries.syntax:
import os
os.getcwd()
os.path.basename(path)
os.path.dirname(path)
os.path.join(folder, subfolder, file)
os.path.exists(path)
entries.example:
import os

print("cwd:", os.getcwd())

some_path = "/Users/clark_kent/data.csv"
print("basename:", os.path.basename(some_path))
print("dirname :", os.path.dirname(some_path))
print("joined  :", os.path.join("data", "raw", "file.csv"))
print("exists? :", os.path.exists("iris.csv"), os.path.exists("nope.csv"))
entries.output:
cwd: /content
basename: data.csv
dirname : /Users/clark_kent
joined  : data/raw/file.csv
exists? : True False
entries.gotcha: Build paths with `os.path.join`, not with `+` and a hard-coded `/`: Windows uses backslashes and the join picks the right one.

entries.title: import … as …
entries.summary: Loads a library and gives it a short alias; `np` for NumPy and `pd` for pandas are conventions the whole community follows.
entries.syntax:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from os.path import join      # one name out of a module
entries.example:
import numpy as np           # the whole library, under a short alias
import pandas as pd
from os.path import join     # one name out of a module

print(np.array([1, 2, 3]) * 2)
print(join("data", "raw", "file.csv"))
print(pd.__name__)
entries.gotcha: Imports live at the top of the notebook in the Setup cell. `NameError: name 'np' is not defined` means that cell has not been run in this session.

entries.title: np.random.seed, randint, randn
entries.summary: NumPy generates random numbers; fixing the seed first makes the “random” draws repeat exactly, which keeps results reproducible.
entries.syntax:
np.random.seed(0)
np.random.randint(low, high, size)     # integers in [low, high)
np.random.randn(n)                     # n draws from a standard normal
entries.example:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)                  # reproducible randomness
print(np.random.randint(1, 7, 10))  # 10 dice rolls

np.random.seed(1)
z = np.random.randn(5)             # 5 draws from a standard normal
print(z.round(2))
entries.gotcha: `high` is excluded: dice need `randint(1, 7)`, not `randint(1, 6)`. Set the seed in the same cell as the draw, or re-running cells in a different order changes the numbers.

entries.title: np.array — create an ndarray; .shape and .dtype
entries.summary: An ndarray is a grid of numbers of one type. Build it from a list (or a list of lists); `.shape` gives (rows, columns).
entries.syntax:
np.array([1, 2, 3])
np.array([[2, 3, 1],
          [3, 1, 2]])
arr.shape      arr.dtype      arr.ndim
entries.example:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([[2, 3, 1],
              [3, 1, 2]])
print(x)
print("shape:", x.shape)      # (2, 3) -> 2 rows, 3 columns
print("dtype:", x.dtype)
print("ndim :", x.ndim)

v = np.array([1.5, 2.5])
print(v.shape, v.dtype)
entries.gotcha: One type per array: mixing `1` and `"a"` turns everything into text. A shape of `(3,)` is a 1-D vector, which is different from a `(3, 1)` column.

entries.title: Vectorized math: operate on the whole array at once
entries.summary: Arithmetic on an array applies to every element, with no loop; two arrays of the same shape combine element by element.
entries.syntax:
arr * 2
arr + other
1 / arr
(arr - 32) * 5 / 9
entries.example:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([[2, 3, 1],
              [3, 1, 2]])
print(x * 2)        # scale every element
print("---")
print(x + x)        # element-wise addition
print("---")
print(1 / x)        # element-wise reciprocal

temps = np.array([68, 71, 65])
print(((temps - 32) * 5 / 9).round(1))     # Fahrenheit -> Celsius
entries.gotcha: A plain list does not do this: `[1, 2, 3] * 2` repeats the list to `[1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]`. Convert with `np.array` first.

entries.title: np.zeros, np.ones, np.identity, np.arange
entries.summary: Ready-made arrays: all zeros or ones of a given shape, an identity matrix, and `arange`, which is `range` as an array.
entries.syntax:
np.zeros((rows, cols))
np.ones((rows, cols))
np.identity(n)
np.arange(start, stop, step)
entries.example:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros((2, 3)))      # all zeros, shape 2x3
print(np.ones((2, 3)))       # all ones
print(np.identity(3))        # 3x3 identity matrix
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2))   # like range, but an array
entries.gotcha: The shape is one argument, a tuple: `np.zeros((2, 3))` with double parentheses. `np.zeros(2, 3)` is an error.

entries.title: Index and slice arrays: a[1:3], m[0, 2], m[:, -1]
entries.summary: Works like list indexing, extended to two dimensions with a comma: `[row, column]`, where `:` means “all”.
entries.syntax:
a[1:3]         # positions 1 and 2
m[0, 2]        # row 0, column 2
m[0, :]        # the whole first row
m[:, -1]       # the whole last column
m[1:, :2]      # rows from 1 on, first two columns
entries.example:
import numpy as np

z = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(z[1:3])
print(z[-1])

m = np.array([[10, 20, 30],
              [40, 50, 60]])
print("element [0,2]:", m[0, 2])
print("first row    :", m[0, :])
print("last column  :", m[:, -1])
print("corner       :", m[1:, :2])
entries.output:
[20 30]
50
element [0,2]: 30
first row    : [10 20 30]
last column  : [30 60]
corner       : [[40 50]]
entries.gotcha: For arrays use one pair of brackets with a comma, `m[0, 2]`; the list style `m[0][2]` works but is slower and does not support `:` across rows.

entries.title: Boolean indexing: z[z > 0]
entries.summary: A comparison on an array gives an array of `True`/`False`; putting it inside the brackets keeps only the `True` positions. This is the foundation of every filter in the course.
entries.syntax:
mask = arr > 0
arr[mask]
arr[arr > 0]
arr[arr % 2 == 0]
entries.example:
import numpy as np

z = np.array([-1.5, 0.8, -0.3, 2.1, 0.4])
print(z > 0)                 # a boolean array
print(z[z > 0])              # keep only the positives

w = np.arange(1, 11)
print(w[w % 2 == 0])         # even numbers
print(w[w > 5].mean())       # mean of the numbers above 5
entries.gotcha: Combine conditions with `&` and `|` and parentheses: `w[(w > 2) & (w < 8)]`. The words `and`/`or` do not work on arrays.

entries.title: Array summaries: .mean(), .max(), .sum(axis=0), .round()
entries.summary: Arrays carry their own statistics as methods; `axis=0` summarizes down the columns, `axis=1` across the rows.
entries.syntax:
arr.mean()   arr.max()   arr.min()   arr.sum()   arr.std()
arr.sum(axis=0)     # per column
arr.mean(axis=1)    # per row
arr.round(2)
entries.example:
import numpy as np

m = np.array([[10, 20, 30],
              [40, 50, 60]])
print("mean:", m.mean(), "| max:", m.max(), "| min:", m.min())
print("column sums:", m.sum(axis=0))
print("row means  :", m.mean(axis=1))
print((m / 7).round(2))
entries.gotcha: In a notebook a bare `m.mean()` displays as `np.float64(35.0)`; `print()` shows plain `35.0`. It is the same number, a NumPy float.

entries.title: Count matches: (arr > 100).sum()
entries.summary: `True` counts as 1, so summing a boolean mask counts how many elements satisfy the condition. The same trick works on pandas columns.
entries.syntax:
(arr > value).sum()
(df["col"] > value).sum()
(mask).mean()          # the proportion that match
entries.example:
import numpy as np

image = np.array([[10, 200, 90],
                  [255, 128, 0],
                  [60, 75, 240]])
bright = image > 100
print(bright)
print("pixels brighter than 100:", bright.sum())
print("share brighter than 100 :", round(bright.mean(), 2))
entries.output:
[[False  True False]
 [ True  True False]
 [False False  True]]
pixels brighter than 100: 4
share brighter than 100 : 0.44
entries.gotcha: `len(image[image > 100])` gives the same count but builds a new array first; `.sum()` on the mask is the idiom you will see in the solutions.
entries.source: hudm5001_mini/assignment_solutions/02 C1, C3, C4; 03 C2; 05 C2

entries.title: pd.Series — a labeled column
entries.summary: A Series is a one-dimensional column of values with a label (the index) beside each one; underneath it is still a NumPy array, so vectorized math and boolean masks carry over.
entries.syntax:
pd.Series([values], index=[labels])
s["label"]        s.iloc[0]        s[s > 70]
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

temps = pd.Series([68, 71, 65, 74], index=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu"])
print(temps)
print("by label   :", temps["Wed"])
print("by position:", temps.iloc[0])
print("mean:", temps.mean(), "| max:", temps.max())
print(temps[temps > 70])           # boolean filtering, exactly like NumPy
entries.output:
Mon    68
Tue    71
Wed    65
Thu    74
dtype: int64
by label   : 65
by position: 68
mean: 69.5 | max: 74
Tue    71
Thu    74
dtype: int64
entries.gotcha: A column of a DataFrame is a Series, so everything here applies to `df["col"]`. The `dtype` line at the bottom is part of the display, not a value.

entries.title: pd.DataFrame from a dict of lists
entries.summary: A DataFrame is a table: each dictionary key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values. Pass `index=` to name the rows.
entries.syntax:
pd.DataFrame({"col1": [...], "col2": [...]})
pd.DataFrame({...}, index=["a", "b"])
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":  ["Maya", "Liam", "Noah"],
    "major": ["Applied Stats", "Learning Analytics", "Measurement"],
    "gpa":   [3.8, 3.5, 3.9],
})
print(students)
print("shape  :", students.shape)
print("columns:", list(students.columns))
print(type(students["gpa"]))          # one column is a Series

weather = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["NYC", "LA"], "temp": [55, 72]}, index=["a", "b"])
print(weather)
entries.output:
name               major  gpa
0  Maya       Applied Stats  3.8
1  Liam  Learning Analytics  3.5
2  Noah         Measurement  3.9
shape  : (3, 3)
columns: ['name', 'major', 'gpa']
<class 'pandas.core.series.Series'>
  city  temp
a  NYC    55
b   LA    72
entries.gotcha: Every list must have the same length, or you get `ValueError: All arrays must be of the same length`.

entries.title: pd.read_csv — load a CSV from a file or a URL
entries.summary: Reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame. A web address works as well as a local path, which is how the course notebooks load data with nothing to download.
entries.syntax:
pd.read_csv("file.csv")
pd.read_csv("https://.../file.csv")
pd.read_csv("file.csv", index_col=0)     # first column is the row labels
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)
print("shape:", iris.shape)
print("columns:", list(iris.columns))
iris.head()
entries.output:

entries.title: .iloc — rows and columns by position
entries.summary: Integer positions, counted from 0, with the right end excluded, exactly like NumPy.
entries.syntax:
df.iloc[0]            # first row
df.iloc[0:3]          # rows 0, 1, 2
df.iloc[1:3, 0:2]     # rows 1-2, first two columns
entries.example:

print("---")

print("---")

entries.title: .loc — rows and columns by label
entries.summary: Row labels and column names. Unlike positions, a label slice includes its right end, the one place beginners get tripped up.
entries.syntax:
df.loc[label]
df.loc[0:3]                        # labels 0, 1, 2, 3 — included!
df.loc[0:2, ["col_a", "col_b"]]
df.loc[label, "col"]

entries.title: Filter rows with a boolean mask
entries.summary: A comparison on a column gives a Series of `True`/`False`; putting it inside `df[...]` keeps only the `True` rows. The move you will use every day.
entries.syntax:
mask = df["col"] > 5
df[mask]
df[df["col"] > 5]
df[df["col"] == "setosa"]
entries.example:
mask = iris["petal_length"] > 4.6
print(mask)

big = iris[mask]
print(big)
print("rows kept:", big.shape[0])

print(iris[iris["species"] == "setosa"])

entries.title: Combine conditions with & and | (in parentheses)
entries.summary: pandas uses `&` for and, `|` for or, and `~` for not, each condition wrapped in parentheses. The words `and`/`or` only work on single values.
entries.syntax:
df[(cond1) & (cond2)]
df[(cond1) | (cond2)]
df[~(cond1)]
entries.example:
both = iris[(iris["species"] == "virginica") & (iris["sepal_length"] >= 6.0)]
print(both)

either = iris[(iris["petal_length"] < 1.5) | (iris["petal_length"] > 5.5)]
print("either:", either.shape[0], "rows")

not_setosa = iris[~(iris["species"] == "setosa")]
print("not setosa:", not_setosa.shape[0], "rows")

4           6.3           6.0  virginica

not setosa: 4 rows
entries.gotcha: Without the parentheses, `&` grabs the numbers before the comparison runs and you get a confusing `TypeError`. Using `and` gives “The truth value of a Series is ambiguous”.

entries.title: Create a column by assignment
entries.summary: Assign to a new name in square brackets. The arithmetic runs on the whole column at once, and a comparison gives a `True`/`False` column with no `if` needed.
entries.syntax:
df["new"] = df["a"] * df["b"]
df["flag"] = df["a"] > df["a"].mean()
entries.example:
iris["petal_area"] = iris["petal_length"] * iris["petal_width"]
iris["big_petal"] = iris["petal_length"] > iris["petal_length"].mean()

entries.title: value_counts() — tally a column
entries.summary: Counts how often each value appears, most frequent first; `normalize=True` gives proportions. `.unique()` lists the distinct values and `.nunique()` counts them.

df["col"].value_counts()
df["col"].value_counts(normalize=True)
df["col"].unique()
df["col"].nunique()

entries.title: groupby() — one statistic per group
entries.summary: Split the rows by the values of one column, compute a statistic inside each group, and stack the answers back up: split–apply–combine in one line.

df.groupby("group_col")["value_col"].mean()
df.groupby("group_col")[["a", "b"]].mean()

entries.title: sort_values() — order the rows
entries.summary: Sorts the table by one column (or several), ascending by default; `ascending=False` puts the largest first, and `.head(n)` after it gives the top n.
entries.syntax:
df.sort_values("col")
df.sort_values("col", ascending=False).head(3)
df.sort_values(["a", "b"])

print(iris.sort_values("petal_length", ascending=False).head(3))

entries.title: Missing values: .isna().sum(), .dropna(), .fillna()
entries.summary: pandas marks a missing value as `NaN`. Count the gaps per column, drop the rows that have one, or fill them with a value such as the column mean.
entries.syntax:
df.isna().sum()
df.dropna()
df.fillna(value)
df["col"].fillna(df["col"].mean())
entries.example:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

demo = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":  ["Ann", "Bob", "Cara"],
    "score": [90, np.nan, 88],
})
print(demo)
print("missing per column:")
print(demo.isna().sum())
print("drop the row with a hole:")
print(demo.dropna())
print("or fill it with the column mean:")
print(demo.fillna(demo["score"].mean()))

entries.title: to_csv(index=False) — save a table
entries.summary: Writes the DataFrame to a CSV file. `index=False` stops pandas from adding a column of row numbers that would come back as a stray column on re-read.
entries.syntax: df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False)
entries.example:
iris.to_csv("iris_out.csv", index=False)
print(open("iris_out.csv").read())              # the file's text
print("re-read shape:", pd.read_csv("iris_out.csv").shape)
entries.gotcha: In Colab the file lands in the session's folder (see the Files panel) and disappears when the runtime ends. Download it if you need it.

entries.title: Series → array or list: .values, np.array(), .to_list()
entries.summary: A column can be handed back to NumPy or plain Python when you want array math or a list.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].values
np.array(df["col"])
df["col"].to_list()
entries.example:
petals = np.array(iris["petal_length"])
print(petals)
print(type(petals).__name__)
print("above the mean:", (petals > petals.mean()).sum())

print(iris["species"].to_list())
entries.gotcha: Usually you do not need the conversion: `iris["petal_length"].mean()` works directly on the Series. Convert when a function insists on a NumPy array or a list.

entries.title: .agg([...]) — pick your own statistics
entries.summary: Instead of taking `describe()` as-is, name the statistics you want in a list and get exactly those, for one column or several.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std", "min", "max"])
df[["a", "b"]].agg(["mean", "median"])
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
    "survived": [0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0],
    "pclass":   [3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 3],
    "sex":      ["male", "female", "female", "female", "male", "male"],
    "age":      [22.0, 38.0, 26.0, 35.0, 35.0, np.nan],

print(titanic["fare"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std", "min", "max"]).round(2))
print("---")
print(titanic[["age", "fare"]].agg(["mean", "median", "std"]).round(2))

entries.title: Median vs mean on skewed data
entries.summary: When a few very large values drag the mean upward, the median describes a typical row better. Reporting both tells the honest story.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].mean()
df["col"].median()
entries.setup_note: imports and six passengers, one of whom paid the most expensive ticket on the ship
entries.example:
print("fare mean  :", round(titanic["fare"].mean(), 2))
print("fare median:", round(titanic["fare"].median(), 2))
print("age mean   :", round(titanic["age"].mean(), 2))
print("age median :", titanic["age"].median())

fare median: 30.58
age mean   : 35.0
age median : 35.0
entries.gotcha: Mean and median far apart means a skewed column. Report the median (and say so) when a handful of extreme values would mislead your reader.

entries.title: .corr() — correlation grid and one pair
entries.summary: Correlation runs from -1 to +1: how two numeric columns move together. On a DataFrame you get the whole grid; on one column with another as the argument you get a single number.
entries.syntax:
df[["a", "b", "c"]].corr()
df["a"].corr(df["b"])
entries.example:
print(titanic[["age", "fare", "pclass", "survived"]].corr().round(2))
print("fare vs pclass:", round(titanic["fare"].corr(titanic["pclass"]), 3))

fare      0.65  1.00   -0.78      0.41
pclass   -0.10 -0.78    1.00     -0.71
survived -0.20  0.41   -0.71      1.00

entries.gotcha: The diagonal is always 1.00 (a column with itself). Text columns are skipped, and a negative number just means the two move in opposite directions.

entries.title: df.copy() — work on a copy, keep the original
entries.summary: `tidy = titanic` is just a second name for the same table; changes show up in both. `.copy()` makes an independent table you can clean without touching the original.
entries.syntax: tidy = df.copy()
entries.example:
alias = titanic                 # another name for the SAME table
alias["note"] = "hi"            # ...so this changes titanic too
print("note column in titanic?", "note" in titanic.columns)

safe = titanic.copy()           # an independent table
safe["flag"] = 1
print("flag column in titanic?", "flag" in titanic.columns)
print(list(safe.columns))

flag column in titanic? False
['passenger_id', 'fare', 'note', 'flag']
entries.gotcha: The same aliasing trap as lists in week 2. Filtering already returns a new table, but when you build on a table you also keep, copy first.

entries.title: .rename(columns={...})
entries.summary: Gives columns readable names with a dictionary of old → new; the result is a new table, so assign it back.
entries.syntax: df = df.rename(columns={"old": "new", "old2": "new2"})
entries.setup_note: imports and a 3-row table with cryptic column names
entries.example:
tidy = titanic.rename(columns={"sibsp": "n_siblings_spouses", "parch": "n_parents_children"})
print(list(tidy.columns))
print(list(titanic.columns))     # the original is unchanged
entries.gotcha: A misspelled old name is silently ignored rather than raising an error, so print the columns afterwards to check.

entries.title: .drop(columns=[...])
entries.summary: Removes columns you do not need (or rows, with `index=`) and returns a new table.
entries.syntax:
df.drop(columns=["a", "b"])
df.drop(index=[0, 1])
df.drop(["a"], axis=1)          # older spelling: axis=1 means columns
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "sibsp": [1, 1, 0],
    "parch": [0, 0, 0],
    "fare": [7.25, 71.28, 7.92],
})
entries.example:
slim = titanic.drop(columns=["sibsp", "parch"])
print(list(slim.columns))
print(titanic.drop(index=[0]))
entries.gotcha: `drop` does not change the original unless you assign the result back (or pass `inplace=True`, which the course avoids).

entries.title: .astype() — change a column's type
entries.summary: Converts a whole column: numbers to text, text to numbers, floats to integers. A 0/1 code that is really a category is a common case.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].astype(str)
df["col"].astype(int)
df["col"].astype(float)
entries.setup_note: imports and a 3-row table where fare came in as text
entries.example:
print("before:", titanic["survived"].dtype)
as_text = titanic["survived"].astype(str)
print("after :", as_text.dtype)

titanic["fare"] = titanic["fare"].astype(float)
print("fare mean:", round(titanic["fare"].mean(), 2))
print(titanic.dtypes)
entries.output:
before: int64
after : object
fare mean: 28.82
survived      int64
pclass        int64
fare        float64
dtype: object
entries.gotcha: `astype(int)` fails on a column with `NaN` (there is no integer NaN). Fill or drop the gaps first.

entries.title: .duplicated().sum() and .drop_duplicates()
entries.summary: Counts exact repeat rows, then removes them; worth running on any dataset before you trust a count.
entries.syntax:
df.duplicated().sum()
df.drop_duplicates()
entries.setup_note: imports and a table where one row was accidentally entered twice
entries.example:
print("duplicate rows:", titanic.duplicated().sum())
no_dupes = titanic.drop_duplicates()
print("rows before:", titanic.shape[0], "| after:", no_dupes.shape[0])
print(no_dupes)

0             1    male   7.25
1             2  female  71.28
2             3  female   7.92
entries.gotcha: Only rows that match in every column count as duplicates. Two different passengers with the same fare are not duplicates.

entries.title: .dropna(subset=[...]) — drop rows missing a specific column
entries.summary: Plain `dropna()` removes a row if any column is missing; `subset=` limits the check to the columns you care about.
entries.syntax:
df.dropna()
df.dropna(subset=["col"])
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "age":      [22.0, np.nan, 26.0, 35.0],
    "embarked": ["S", "C", np.nan, "S"],
})
entries.setup_note: imports and a table with one missing age and one missing port
entries.example:
print(titanic.isna().sum())
print("dropna()             ->", titanic.dropna().shape[0], "rows")
print("dropna(subset=[age]) ->", titanic.dropna(subset=["age"]).shape[0], "rows")
print(titanic.dropna(subset=["age"]))

age             1
embarked        1

dropna(subset=[age]) -> 3 rows
