0             1  22.0        S
2             3  26.0      NaN
3             4  35.0        S
entries.gotcha: Dropping is easy to overdo: with many columns almost every row has some gap somewhere, and `dropna()` can throw away most of your data.

entries.title: .fillna() with the column median
entries.summary: Fills the gaps in a column with a chosen value, typically the median for a skewed numeric column or the most common value for a category.
entries.syntax:
df["col"] = df["col"].fillna(df["col"].median())
df["col"] = df["col"].fillna("S")
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    "age":      [22.0, 38.0, np.nan, 35.0, 54.0],
    "embarked": ["S", "C", "S", np.nan, "S"],
})
entries.setup_note: imports and a table with one missing age and one missing port
entries.example:
filled = titanic.copy()
filled["age"] = filled["age"].fillna(filled["age"].median())
filled["embarked"] = filled["embarked"].fillna("S")
print(filled)
print("gaps left:", filled.isna().sum().sum())
entries.output:
passenger_id   age embarked
0             1  22.0        S
1             2  38.0        C
2             3  36.5        S
3             4  35.0        S
4             5  54.0        S
gaps left: 0
entries.gotcha: Filling keeps every row but invents values. Count the gaps before you fill (`isna().sum()`) and mention the number in your write-up.

entries.title: groupby() + .agg([...]) — several statistics per group
entries.summary: Pair `groupby` with a list of statistics and you get a real descriptive table: one row per group, one column per statistic.
entries.syntax: df.groupby("g")["x"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std"])
entries.example:
# the mean of a 0/1 column IS the proportion who survived
print(titanic.groupby("pclass")["survived"].mean().round(3))
print("---")
print(titanic.groupby("pclass")["fare"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std"]).round(2))
entries.output:
pclass
1    1.00
3    0.25
Name: survived, dtype: float64
---
        count   mean  median    std
pclass
1           2  62.19   62.19  12.86
3           4   7.92    7.98   0.50
entries.gotcha: The statistics are computed within each group, so `std` is the spread inside class 1, inside class 3, and so on, not the overall spread.

entries.title: Group by two keys
entries.summary: Pass a list of columns to `groupby` and you get one row per combination of their values.
entries.syntax: df.groupby(["a", "b"])["x"].mean()
entries.example: print(titanic.groupby(["pclass", "sex"])["survived"].mean().round(3))
entries.output:
pclass  sex
1       female    1.0
        male      0.5
3       female    1.0
        male      0.0
Name: survived, dtype: float64
entries.gotcha: The result has a two-level index, which reads fine but is awkward to use; `pivot_table` lays the same numbers out as a grid.

entries.title: Group sizes: .size() vs .count()
entries.summary: `.size()` counts the rows in each group; `["col"].count()` counts only the non-missing values of that column, so the two differ by the number of gaps.
entries.syntax:
df.groupby("g").size()
df.groupby("g")["col"].count()
entries.setup_note: imports and six passengers, one with no recorded age
entries.example:
print(titanic.groupby("pclass").size())
print("---")
print(titanic.groupby("pclass")["age"].count())
entries.output:
pclass
1    2
3    4
dtype: int64
---
pclass
1    2
3    3
Name: age, dtype: int64
entries.gotcha: SQL's `COUNT(*)` behaves like `.size()`; pandas' `.count()` behaves like `COUNT(col)`. When a SQL summary and a pandas summary disagree, this is the first place to look.

entries.title: .to_dict() — a summary back into plain Python
entries.summary: Turns a Series (such as a group summary) into an ordinary dictionary, ready for f-strings, loops or JSON.
entries.syntax: df.groupby("g")["x"].mean().to_dict()
entries.example:
fare_by_class = titanic.groupby("pclass")["fare"].mean().round(2).to_dict()
print(fare_by_class)
print("first class paid on average:", fare_by_class[1])
entries.gotcha: The values are still NumPy numbers; wrap them in `float()` before `json.dump`.

entries.title: pd.pivot_table — a summary laid out as a grid
entries.summary: One grouping variable down the side, another across the top, and a statistic in each cell: the same numbers as a two-key groupby, far easier to read.
entries.syntax: pd.pivot_table(df, values="x", index="row_var", columns="col_var", aggfunc="mean")
entries.example:
grid = pd.pivot_table(titanic,
                      values="survived",
                      index="pclass",      # rows
                      columns="sex",       # columns
                      aggfunc="mean").round(3)
print(grid)
entries.gotcha: The default `aggfunc` is the mean. Say `aggfunc="count"` or `"sum"` explicitly when you want something else.

entries.title: groupby drops rows with a missing key
entries.summary: Rows whose grouping value is `NaN` belong to no group, so `groupby` and `pivot_table` leave them out without a warning.
entries.syntax: df.groupby("g")["x"].count().sum()   # compare with df.shape[0]
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 62],
    "survived": [0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1],
    "embarked": ["S", "C", "S", "S", "S", np.nan],
})
entries.setup_note: imports and six passengers, one with no port recorded
entries.example:
grouped_total = titanic.groupby("embarked")["survived"].count().sum()
print("rows in the table :", titanic.shape[0])
print("rows in the groups:", grouped_total, " <- the passenger with no port fell out")
entries.output:
rows in the table : 6
rows in the groups: 5  <- the passenger with no port fell out
entries.gotcha: Check that group totals add up to the row count whenever the grouping column has gaps. `groupby("embarked", dropna=False)` keeps them as their own group.

entries.title: pd.concat — stack tables
entries.summary: Glues tables together: `axis=0` stacks rows (the default), `axis=1` places them side by side. `ignore_index=True` renumbers the rows.
entries.syntax:
pd.concat([a, b], axis=0, ignore_index=True)     # rows
pd.concat([a, b], axis=1)                        # columns
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

school_1 = pd.DataFrame({"stu_id": [101, 102], "sch_id": [1, 1]})
school_2 = pd.DataFrame({"stu_id": [103, 104, 105], "sch_id": [2, 2, 2]})

students = pd.concat([school_1, school_2], axis=0, ignore_index=True)   # stack vertically
print(students)

info = pd.DataFrame({"GPA": [3.1, 2.5, 3.2, 3.7, 2.9]})
print(pd.concat([students, info], axis=1))                             # side by side
entries.gotcha: Without `ignore_index=True` the stacked table keeps the old labels (0, 1, 0, 1, 2), which confuses `.loc` later. Side-by-side concat matches rows by label, not by position.

entries.title: pd.merge(on=, how=) — join two tables on a key
entries.summary: Matches the rows of two tables that share a value in the key column and lines their columns up, exactly like a SQL join.
entries.syntax: pd.merge(left, right, on="key", how="left")
entries.output:
shape before: (4, 2) -> after: (4, 4)
   passenger_id embarked    port_name  country
0             1        S  Southampton  England
1             2        C    Cherbourg   France
2             3        S  Southampton  England
3             4        Q   Queenstown  Ireland
entries.gotcha: `merge` joins on a shared column; `concat` just stacks. If the key has different names in the two tables use `left_on=` and `right_on=`.

entries.title: how= left / right / inner / outer, and the row-count check
entries.summary: `how` decides what happens to rows without a match: `left` keeps every left row (filling with `NaN`), `inner` keeps only matches, `outer` keeps everything from both sides.
entries.syntax:
pd.merge(a, b, on="k", how="left")
pd.merge(a, b, on="k", how="inner")
pd.merge(a, b, on="k", how="outer")
entries.setup_note: imports, four passengers (one with no port) and the ports lookup
entries.example:
left = pd.merge(titanic, ports, on="embarked", how="left")
inner = pd.merge(titanic, ports, on="embarked", how="inner")
print("left join rows :", left.shape[0])
print("inner join rows:", inner.shape[0], " <- passenger 62 is gone")
print(left)
entries.output:
left join rows : 4
inner join rows: 3  <- passenger 62 is gone
   passenger_id embarked    port_name
0             1        S  Southampton
1             2        C    Cherbourg
2             3        S  Southampton
3            62      NaN          NaN
entries.gotcha: Check the row count after every join. If it changed and you did not expect it to, something is wrong with the key.

entries.title: pd.get_dummies — one-hot encode a category
entries.summary: Turns a text column into one 0/1 column per category, the form models need instead of labels.
entries.syntax:
pd.get_dummies(df["col"])
pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["col"])
pd.get_dummies(df["col"], drop_first=True, prefix="col")
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

cats = pd.DataFrame({"breed": ["persian", "persian", "siamese", "himalayan", "burmese"]})
print(pd.get_dummies(cats, columns=["breed"]))
print("---")
print(pd.get_dummies(cats["breed"], drop_first=True, prefix="breed").astype(int))
entries.output:
breed_burmese  breed_himalayan  breed_persian  breed_siamese
0          False            False           True          False
1          False            False           True          False
2          False            False          False           True
3          False             True          False          False
4           True            False          False          False
---
   breed_himalayan  breed_persian  breed_siamese
0                0              1              0
1                0              1              0
2                0              0              1
3                1              0              0
4                0              0              0
entries.gotcha: Recent pandas returns `True`/`False` columns; add `.astype(int)` for 0/1. `drop_first=True` removes one redundant column, which regression models prefer.

entries.title: .apply(lambda ...) — run a function down a column
entries.summary: Applies a function to every value of a column (or, with `axis=1`, to every row) and returns the results as a new Series. Its natural partner is a lambda.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].apply(function)
df["col"].apply(lambda x: x ** 2)
df.apply(lambda row: row["a"] + row["b"], axis=1)
entries.example:
iris["sepal_len_sq"] = iris["sepal_length"].apply(lambda x: x ** 2)

# row-wise: axis=1 hands each row to the function
iris["sepal_avg"] = iris[["sepal_length", "sepal_width"]].apply(lambda r: r.mean(), axis=1)

iris["label"] = iris["species"].apply(lambda s: s[:3].upper())
print(iris)
entries.output:
sepal_length  sepal_width     species  sepal_len_sq  sepal_avg label
0           5.1          3.5      setosa         26.01       4.30   SET
1           4.9          3.0      setosa         24.01       3.95   SET
2           7.0          3.2  versicolor         49.00       5.10   VER
entries.gotcha: For plain arithmetic, `iris["sepal_length"] ** 2` is simpler and faster than `apply`. Reach for `apply` when the function is not vectorized, such as text logic or a custom rule.

entries.title: sqlite3.connect() and .cursor()
entries.summary: `connect` opens a database file (creating it if needed) and returns a connection; a cursor runs statements on it. `sqlite3` is built into Python.
entries.syntax:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")      # a file
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")       # temporary, in memory
cur = conn.cursor()
entries.example:
import sqlite3
import os

conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")    # creates the file if it is not there yet
cur = conn.cursor()
print(type(conn).__name__, "/", type(cur).__name__)
print("file created:", os.path.exists("course.db"))
conn.close()
entries.gotcha: The database is a real file in your working folder. In Colab it disappears with the runtime, like any other file; download it if you need it later.

entries.title: cur.execute(sql) then conn.commit()
entries.summary: `execute` runs one SQL statement; `commit` saves the changes to the file. The notebook pattern: connect → cursor → execute → commit.
entries.syntax:
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE ...")
conn.commit()
entries.example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
cur = conn.cursor()

cur.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS holdings")          # start clean so the cell can be re-run
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL)")
conn.commit()

print(cur.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'").fetchall())
conn.close()
entries.gotcha: Forgetting `commit()` means the changes may never reach the file. Re-running a cell with `CREATE TABLE` fails unless a `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` comes first.

entries.title: cur.executemany() with ? placeholders
entries.summary: Inserts many rows in one call from a list of tuples; the `?` marks are filled in safely by SQLite, so values never get pasted into the query text.
entries.syntax:
rows = [(v1, v2, v3), (v1, v2, v3)]
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?, ?)", rows)
conn.commit()
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS holdings")
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL)")
conn.commit()
entries.setup_note: a connection and an empty holdings table
entries.example:
stocks = [
    ("NVDA", 219.00, -3.42),
    ("AAPL", 146.00, -2.73),
    ("GOOG", 2829.27, -58.20),
]
cur.execute("DELETE FROM holdings")                       # so re-running does not pile up duplicates
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO holdings VALUES (?, ?, ?)", stocks)
conn.commit()
print("rows inserted:", cur.rowcount)
print(cur.execute("SELECT * FROM holdings").fetchall())
entries.gotcha: One `?` per column, and the data must be a list of tuples, one tuple per row. Never build the query with f-strings and pasted values.

entries.title: .fetchall() — query results as a list of tuples
entries.summary: Run a `SELECT` on the cursor and `fetchall()` returns every row as a tuple in a list; or loop over `conn.execute(query)` one row at a time.
entries.syntax:
rows = cur.execute("SELECT ...").fetchall()
rows[0][0]                       # first row, first column
for row in conn.execute("SELECT ..."):
    print(row)
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS holdings")
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL)")
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO holdings VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [("NVDA", 219.0, -3.42), ("AAPL", 146.0, -2.73), ("GOOG", 2829.27, -58.2)])
conn.commit()
entries.setup_note: a connection and a holdings table with three rows
entries.example:
rows = cur.execute("SELECT ticker, price FROM holdings WHERE price > 200").fetchall()
print(rows)
print("first ticker:", rows[0][0])       # a list of tuples, indexed as usual

for row in conn.execute("SELECT * FROM holdings"):
    print(row)
entries.gotcha: Column names are not included; you get positions only. When you want names, read the query with `pd.read_sql_query` instead.

entries.title: pd.read_sql_query(query, conn) — results as a DataFrame
entries.summary: The friendliest way to run SQL: the result comes back as a DataFrame with column names, so everything from the pandas weeks applies.
entries.syntax:
pd.read_sql_query("SELECT ...", conn)
pd.read_sql("SELECT ...", conn)        # same thing, shorter name
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS holdings")
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL)")
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO holdings VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [("NVDA", 219.0, -3.42), ("AAPL", 146.0, -2.73), ("GOOG", 2829.27, -58.2)])
conn.commit()
entries.setup_note: a connection and a holdings table with three rows
entries.example:
query = """
SELECT ticker, price
FROM holdings
WHERE price > 200
ORDER BY price DESC
"""
df = pd.read_sql_query(query, conn)
print(type(df).__name__)
print(df)
print("mean price:", df["price"].mean())
entries.output:
DataFrame
  ticker    price
0   GOOG  2829.27
1   NVDA   219.00
mean price: 1524.135
entries.gotcha: The first argument is the SQL text, the second the connection; swapping them raises an error. Write long queries in a triple-quoted string.

entries.title: df.to_sql() — write a DataFrame into the database
entries.summary: One line turns a whole DataFrame into a table, the bridge between the pandas half and the SQL half of the course.
entries.syntax: df.to_sql("table_name", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
ports = pd.DataFrame({
    "embarked":  ["S", "C", "Q"],
    "port_name": ["Southampton", "Cherbourg", "Queenstown"],
    "country":   ["England", "France", "Ireland"],
})
entries.setup_note: a connection and the ports DataFrame
entries.example:
ports.to_sql("ports", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
conn.commit()

print(pd.read_sql_query("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'", conn))
print(pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM ports WHERE country = 'France'", conn))
entries.output:
name
0  ports
  embarked  port_name country
0        C  Cherbourg  France
entries.gotcha: `if_exists="replace"` lets the cell be re-run; the default (`"fail"`) raises an error the second time. `index=False` keeps the row numbers out of the table.

entries.title: Which tables are in the database?
entries.summary: SQLite keeps its own catalog in `sqlite_master`; query it from pandas to see the tables.
entries.syntax: pd.read_sql_query("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'", conn)
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
pd.DataFrame({"a": [1]}).to_sql("passengers", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
pd.DataFrame({"b": [1]}).to_sql("ports", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
conn.commit()
entries.setup_note: a connection with two small tables in it
entries.example: print(pd.read_sql_query("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'", conn))
entries.gotcha: An empty result means the tables were never committed, or the connection points at a different file than you think (check with `os.getcwd()`).

entries.title: conn.commit() and conn.close()
entries.summary: Commit saves, close releases the file. The database file stays on disk afterwards, ready to be opened again.
entries.syntax:
conn.commit()
conn.close()
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
import os
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (txt TEXT)")
entries.example:
conn.commit()
conn.close()
print("connection closed")
print("the database file is still on disk:", os.path.exists("course.db"))

# reopen later and the data is still there
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
print(conn.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'").fetchall())
conn.close()
entries.output:
connection closed
the database file is still on disk: True
[('notes',)]
entries.gotcha: Using a closed connection raises `ProgrammingError: Cannot operate on a closed database`. Open a new one with `sqlite3.connect`.

entries.title: A multi-line query in a triple-quoted string
entries.summary: Triple quotes let a query span several lines, one clause per line, which is how every longer query in the course is written.
entries.syntax:
query = """
SELECT ...
FROM ...
WHERE ...
"""
pd.read_sql_query(query, conn)
entries.setup:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
conn = sqlite3.connect("course.db")
pd.DataFrame({
    "pclass": [3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 3],
    "survived": [0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0],
    "fare": [7.25, 71.28, 7.92, 53.10, 8.05, 8.46],
}).to_sql("passengers", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
entries.setup_note: a connection and a passengers table with six rows
entries.example:
query = """
SELECT pclass,
       COUNT(*)                AS n_passengers,
       ROUND(AVG(survived), 3) AS survival_rate,
       ROUND(AVG(fare), 2)     AS avg_fare
FROM passengers
GROUP BY pclass
ORDER BY pclass
"""
print(pd.read_sql_query(query, conn))
entries.gotcha: The string is plain text to Python, so a typo inside it only shows up when SQLite runs it. Read the `OperationalError` message: it names the bad token.

entries.title: if / else — act on a decision
entries.summary: `if` runs its indented block only when the condition is `True`; `else` runs otherwise. The colon and the four-space indent are the grammar.
entries.gotcha: `if score = 60:` is a `SyntaxError`: `=` assigns, `==` compares. Colab indents for you when you type the colon and press Enter.

entries.title: elif ladders: the first true branch wins
entries.summary: Chain conditions with `elif`; Python checks them top to bottom, runs the first that is `True`, and skips the rest. `else` catches everything left over.
entries.gotcha: Order does the work: each rung silently means “and not the ones above”. Reverse the ladder and every score lands on the first rung.

entries.title: One-line choice: x if condition else y
entries.summary: Picks one of two values in a single expression, so it can sit on the right of `=` or inside an f-string.
entries.syntax: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
entries.example:
score = 72
label = "pass" if score >= 60 else "fail"     # reads: label IS "pass" if ... otherwise "fail"
print(label)

age = 71
print(f"passenger status: {'senior' if age >= 65 else 'adult'}")

for n in range(1, 6):
    print(n, "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd")
entries.output:
pass
passenger status: senior
1 odd
2 even
3 odd
4 even
5 odd
entries.gotcha: Both halves are required; `"pass" if score >= 60` alone is a `SyntaxError`. When you feel tempted to nest one inside another, switch back to a full `if`/`elif` ladder.

entries.title: for loop — repeat over an iterable
entries.summary: Walks through the items of a collection one at a time, refilling the loop variable and running the indented block on each pass.
entries.syntax:
for item in collection:
    ...   # indented block runs once per item
entries.example:
programs = ["Applied Stats", "Learning Analytics", "Measurement"]

for program in programs:
    print(program, "->", len(program), "characters")

# a string is an iterable of characters
for ch in "iris":
    print(ch.upper(), end=" ")
print()
entries.output:
Applied Stats -> 13 characters
Learning Analytics -> 18 characters
Measurement -> 11 characters
I R I S
entries.gotcha: Name the loop variable something singular and readable (`for program in programs`). Everything indented belongs to the loop; the first un-indented line runs after it finishes.

entries.title: for i in range(n) — loop a fixed number of times
entries.summary: `range` finally shows its real job: driving a loop without building a list first.
entries.example:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i, "squared is", i ** 2)

for _ in range(3):             # _ when you do not need the counter
    print("hello")
entries.output:
1 squared is 1
2 squared is 4
3 squared is 9
4 squared is 16
5 squared is 25
hello
hello
hello
entries.gotcha: `range(5)` gives 0 to 4, never 5. To count 1 to 5 write `range(1, 6)`.

entries.title: The accumulator pattern: total += x
entries.summary: Create a variable before the loop, update it inside, use it after. This is what `.sum()` and `.mean()` do for you all along.
entries.syntax:
total = 0              # 1. create BEFORE the loop
for x in xs:
    total += x         # 2. update INSIDE (total = total + x)
print(total)           # 3. use AFTER
entries.example:
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95, 84]

total = 0                 # 1. create BEFORE the loop
for s in scores:
    total += s            # 2. update INSIDE the loop
print("total:", total)    # 3. use AFTER the loop
print("mean :", total / len(scores))
entries.gotcha: Putting `total = 0` inside the loop resets it on every pass, so the answer is just the last item.

entries.title: Count with a loop and an if
entries.summary: Swap the running total for a counter and add a condition: the first loop-plus-branch combination, and the bread and butter of everyday programming.
entries.example:
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95, 84]

count = 0
for s in scores:
    if s > 85:
        count += 1
print(count, "scores above 85")

# the vectorized way says the same thing
import numpy as np
print((np.array(scores) > 85).sum())
entries.gotcha: `count += 1` must be indented under the `if`, one level deeper than the `for`, or it counts every item.

entries.title: enumerate(xs, start=1) — position and value
entries.summary: Hands you the position and the item as a pair on each pass, so you never keep a manual counter. `start=1` counts like a human.
entries.syntax:
for i, x in enumerate(xs):
for i, x in enumerate(xs, start=1):
entries.example:
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95, 84]

for rank, s in enumerate(scores, start=1):
    print(f"student {rank}: {s}")

print(list(enumerate(["a", "b"])))      # what it produces: (index, item) pairs
entries.gotcha: The pair unpacks into two loop variables; with only one (`for pair in enumerate(xs)`) you get tuples like `(0, 88)`.

entries.title: zip(xs, ys) — two lists in step
entries.summary: Walks two (or more) lists together, pairing them up element by element.
entries.syntax: for a, b in zip(xs, ys):
entries.example:
names  = ["Ann", "Bob", "Cara", "Dan", "Eve"]
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95, 84]

for name, s in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name} scored {s}")

print(list(zip(names[:2], scores[:2])))
entries.output:
Ann scored 88
Bob scored 92
Cara scored 79
Dan scored 95
Eve scored 84
[('Ann', 88), ('Bob', 92)]
entries.gotcha: `zip` stops at the shorter list without any warning. Check that the lists have the same length first.

entries.title: Best-so-far tracker: find the max and who owns it
entries.summary: Keep a champion variable and replace it whenever the loop meets something better. This is how `max()` works inside, and it also tells you which item won.
entries.example:
names  = ["Ann", "Bob", "Cara", "Dan", "Eve"]
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95, 84]

best_name = ""
best_score = 0
for name, s in zip(names, scores):
    if s > best_score:        # a challenger beats the champion...
        best_score = s        # ...so both trackers update
        best_name = name
print(f"top score: {best_score}, by {best_name}")
entries.gotcha: Start the tracker below every possible value (0 is fine for scores, but not for temperatures that can be negative). Both variables must update together.

entries.title: while loop — repeat until told to stop
entries.summary: Re-runs its block as long as the condition stays `True`; use it when you do not know in advance how many repetitions you need.
entries.syntax:
while condition:
    ...            # something in here must move toward False
entries.example:
ix = 1
while ix < 10:
    ix = ix * 2
    print("ix is now", ix)
print("final:", ix)

# how many years until $1000 doubles at 6%?
balance = 1000
years = 0
while balance < 2000:
    balance = balance * 1.06
    years += 1
print(f"doubled after {years} years, at ${round(balance, 2)}")
entries.output:
ix is now 2
ix is now 4
ix is now 8
ix is now 16
final: 16
doubled after 12 years, at $2012.2
entries.gotcha: If you are walking a collection you already have, use `for`; it cannot loop forever. `while` is for “repeat until something happens”.

entries.title: The infinite loop, and how to avoid it
entries.summary: If nothing inside the loop changes the condition, it never becomes `False` and the cell spins forever. Interrupt, find the variable that never changed, fix, re-run.
entries.syntax:
# WRONG: nothing inside changes ix, so this never ends
ix = 1
while ix < 10:
    print(ix)

# RIGHT: the update moves ix toward the exit
ix = 1
while ix < 10:
    print(ix)
    ix = ix * 2
entries.example:
ix = 1
passes = 0
while ix < 10:
    ix = ix * 2          # the update that makes the loop end
    passes += 1
print("passes:", passes, "| ix:", ix)
entries.gotcha: In Colab, click the cell's stop button or Runtime ▸ Interrupt execution, then look for the missing `+= 1` (or `* 2`) inside the loop.

entries.title: break — stop the whole loop
entries.summary: Abandons the loop right now, usually inside an `if`. Perfect for searches: once you have found what you wanted, stop looking.
entries.gotcha: `break` only leaves the innermost loop it sits in. One well-placed `break` makes code clearer; five make a maze.

entries.title: continue — skip this pass
entries.summary: Abandons the current pass only and jumps to the next item. Perfect for skipping bad or irrelevant entries.
entries.example:
readings = [7.0, None, 6.4, 5.8, None, 7.7]

total = 0
count = 0
for r in readings:
    if r is None:
        continue                   # skip this pass; the two lines below never run
    total += r
    count += 1

print(f"mean of {count} valid readings: {round(total / count, 2)}")
entries.gotcha: In a `while` loop, make sure the counter is updated before the `continue`, or the same item repeats forever.

entries.title: None and `is None`
entries.summary: `None` is Python's “no value”. Test for it with `is None` / `is not None`, the one place `is` is the right comparison.
entries.syntax:
if value is None:
if value is not None:
entries.gotcha: `None` is not the same as `0`, `""` or `NaN`. A function with no `return` hands back `None`, which is why `x = my_list.sort()` leaves `x` empty.

entries.title: iter() and next() — what for really does
entries.summary: An iterable can hand out its items one at a time; `iter()` makes the bookmark (an iterator) and `next()` asks for the next item. `for` does exactly this behind the scenes and stops at `StopIteration`.
entries.syntax:
it = iter(iterable)
next(it)        # the next item; StopIteration when nothing is left
entries.example:
tokens = ["fit", "predict", "score"]

it = iter(tokens)          # a bookmark into the list
print(type(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))            # nothing left -> StopIteration
entries.gotcha: You almost never call `iter`/`next` yourself; the point is to understand why so many different things (lists, strings, ranges, dicts, Series) work in a `for` loop.

entries.title: Iterators are one-shot: list(zip(...))
entries.summary: `zip` and `enumerate` build iterators that produce pairs on demand; walk one once and it is spent. Wrap it in `list()` if you need the items twice.
entries.syntax: pairs = list(zip(xs, ys))     # keep the pairs
entries.example:
pairs = zip(["a", "b", "c"], [1, 2, 3])
print(pairs)             # an iterator object, not a list
print(list(pairs))       # ask for the items -> there they are
print(list(pairs))       # empty! an iterator can be walked only ONCE

kept = list(zip(["a", "b"], [1, 2]))
print(kept, kept)        # a list can be reused
entries.gotcha: The same `list(range(...))` move from week 2: `range`, `zip`, `enumerate` and dict views all become real lists with `list()`.
entries.output_note: The address inside `<zip object at 0x…>` differs every run.

entries.title: Loop over a dict: keys, .values(), .items()
entries.summary: Looping a bare dict gives its keys; `.values()` gives the values; `.items()` gives both, unpacked into two loop variables, which is the form you will use most.
entries.example:
enrollment = {"HUDM 5001": 32, "HUDM 5122": 28, "HUDM 5026": 24}

for course in enrollment:                  # keys
    print(course)

for n in enrollment.values():              # values
    print(n, end=" ")
print()

for course, n in enrollment.items():       # both
    print(f"{course}: {n} students")
entries.output:
HUDM 5001
HUDM 5122
HUDM 5026
32 28 24
HUDM 5001: 32 students
HUDM 5122: 28 students
HUDM 5026: 24 students
entries.gotcha: `for k, v in d:` without `.items()` raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`; the bare dict only yields keys.

entries.title: Loop over a Series with .items()
entries.summary: A group summary is a Series, and a Series has `.items()` like a dict, yielding (label, value) pairs; add an `if` and each group gets a verdict.
entries.syntax:
for label, value in series.items():
for g, m in df.groupby("g")["x"].mean().items():
entries.output:
setosa: 1.4 cm — on the shorter side
versicolor: 4.6 cm — longer than the garden average
virginica: 5.55 cm — longer than the garden average
entries.gotcha: Loop over the summary (a few groups), not over the rows; that is the “loop over things, vectorize over numbers” rule.

entries.title: Audit a table: for col in df.columns
entries.summary: Column names are an iterable of strings, so checking every column of a new dataset takes four lines. The loop you will reuse on every dataset you meet.
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

titanic = pd.DataFrame({
    "passenger_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "age":      [22.0, np.nan, 26.0, np.nan],
    "embarked": ["S", "C", np.nan, "S"],
})
entries.setup_note: imports and a 4-row table with some gaps
entries.gotcha: `titanic.isna().sum()` gives the same numbers in one line; the loop earns its keep when you want a sentence per column or a conditional report.

entries.title: Loop over things, vectorize over numbers
entries.summary: Row-by-row arithmetic in a Python loop is slower than the pandas one-liner by orders of magnitude. Loop over files, columns, groups and report lines; vectorize over rows of numbers.
entries.syntax:
# slow: visiting every row by hand
for i in range(df.shape[0]):
    areas.append(df["a"].iloc[i] * df["b"].iloc[i])

# fast: the whole column at once
areas = df["a"] * df["b"]
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
import time

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)
entries.example:
big = pd.concat([iris] * 200, ignore_index=True)   # 30,000 rows of iris
print("rows:", big.shape[0])

t0 = time.perf_counter()
areas = []
for i in range(big.shape[0]):
    areas.append(big["petal_length"].iloc[i] * big["petal_width"].iloc[i])
loop_secs = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
vec = big["petal_length"] * big["petal_width"]
vec_secs = time.perf_counter() - t0

print("loop      :", round(loop_secs, 4), "s")
print("vectorized:", round(vec_secs, 4), "s")
print(f"same answers? {areas[0] == vec.iloc[0]} — roughly {round(loop_secs / vec_secs)}x slower by hand")
entries.output:
rows: 30000
loop      : 0.0963 s
vectorized: 0.0001 s
same answers? True — roughly 708x slower by hand
entries.output_note: The seconds change from run to run and machine to machine; the story does not.
entries.gotcha: If the body of your loop is arithmetic on a column, stop and write the pandas one-liner instead.

entries.title: df.iterrows() — row by row, as a last resort
entries.summary: Hands you each row's label and the row itself as a Series. Fine for a peek or a rare job with no vectorized equivalent; slow for arithmetic.
entries.syntax:
for idx, row in df.iterrows():
    row["col"]
entries.output:
passenger 1: male, class 3
passenger 2: female, class 1
passenger 3: female, class 3
entries.gotcha: Changing `row` inside the loop does not change the table. For anything numeric, use a column expression instead.

entries.title: time.perf_counter() — time a piece of code
entries.summary: Read the clock before and after, subtract, and you have the elapsed seconds; the way the notebooks race a loop against a vectorized line.
entries.syntax:
import time
t0 = time.perf_counter()
...
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
entries.example:
import time

t0 = time.perf_counter()
total = 0
for i in range(1_000_000):
    total += i
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
print("total:", total)
print("seconds:", round(elapsed, 3))
entries.output_note: Timings vary with the machine; only the total is stable.
entries.gotcha: One run is noisy. When two timings are close, repeat them a few times before drawing a conclusion.

entries.title: Chained comparison: -2 < val < 2 (and the parentheses trap)
entries.summary: Python lets you chain comparisons the way math does. Wrap one side in parentheses and you compare a boolean to a number instead, which is legal and almost never what you meant.
entries.syntax:
-2 < val < 2          # between -2 and 2
(-2 < val) and (val < 2)   # the same, spelled out
entries.example:
val = 5
print(-2 < val < 2)        # False: 5 is not between -2 and 2
print((-2 < val) < 2)      # True: (-2 < 5) is True, and True < 2 is 1 < 2
print(10 <= 15 <= 25)
entries.gotcha: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0 in arithmetic and comparisons, which is why the misplaced parentheses give a confident wrong answer instead of an error.

entries.title: def — define a function
entries.summary: Packages a block of code under a name so it can be called with different inputs; `return` hands a value back to the caller.
entries.syntax:
def function_name(parameter1, parameter2):
    """Docstring: what it does."""
    ...
    return value

result = function_name(arg1, arg2)
entries.gotcha: A function must be defined above the line that calls it. Calling first gives `NameError: name '...' is not defined`. Design each function to do one thing and give it a name that says so.

entries.title: Docstrings, help() and .__doc__
entries.summary: The first triple-quoted string inside a function documents what it does, what goes in and what comes out; `help()` and `.__doc__` show it.
entries.syntax:
def f(x):
    """One line saying what f does."""
    ...

help(f)
print(f.__doc__)
entries.example:
def verify_string_length(text, n):
    """Return True if text has at least n characters."""
    return len(text) >= n

print(verify_string_length.__doc__)
help(verify_string_length)
entries.output:
Return True if text has at least n characters.
Help on function verify_string_length in module __main__:

verify_string_length(text, n)
    Return True if text has at least n characters.
entries.gotcha: The docstring must be the very first statement in the body; a comment above it with `#` is not a docstring and `help()` will not show it.

entries.title: Positional vs keyword arguments
entries.summary: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so order matters; naming them (`x=1, y=2`) lets you pass them in any order and makes calls readable.
entries.syntax:
f(1, 2)          # positional: first -> first parameter
f(y=2, x=1)      # keyword: matched by name
entries.example:
def fcn(x, y):
    return 5 * x + y

print(fcn(1, 2))          # x=1, y=2
print(fcn(2, 1))          # order matters
print(fcn(y=2, x=1))      # keyword arguments can go in any order
entries.gotcha: Too few arguments raises `TypeError: fcn() missing 1 required positional argument`. Positional arguments must come before keyword ones in a call.

entries.title: Default arguments
entries.summary: A parameter with `=value` in the definition is optional; the default is used when the caller leaves it out.
entries.syntax: def f(required, optional=default):
entries.example:
def show_results(precision, printing=True):     # printing has a default
    if printing:
        print(f"precision = {precision}")
    return precision

show_results(0.912)                       # uses the default printing=True
value = show_results(0.912, printing=False)   # silenced
print("returned:", value)
entries.gotcha: Defaults must come after the required parameters: `def f(a, b=1, c)` is a `SyntaxError`. Never use a list or dict as a default (see the classes week).

entries.title: *args — any number of arguments
entries.summary: A parameter written `*name` collects all extra positional arguments into a tuple, so the function accepts one value or twenty.
entries.example:
def square_args(*vars):        # *vars gathers all arguments into a tuple
    print(type(vars), len(vars), "arguments")
    return [v ** 2 for v in vars]

print(square_args(2, 3, 4))
print(square_args(10))

models = ["logreg", "naive_bayes", "gbm"]
print(square_args(*[1, 2, 3]))     # * in the call unpacks the list
entries.gotcha: Inside the function `args` is a tuple even when only one value was passed. The name `args` is a convention; the star is what matters.

entries.title: Return several values, unpack them, ignore with _
entries.summary: `return a, b, c` hands back a tuple; the caller unpacks it into names, using `_` for values it does not need.
entries.syntax:
def f():
    return x, y, z

a, b, c = f()
_, _, last = f()
entries.example:
def negate_coords(x, y, z):
    return -x, -y, -z          # returns a 3-tuple

a, b, c = negate_coords(10, 20, 30)
print(a, b, c)

_, _, last = negate_coords(1, 2, 3)   # keep only the third value
print(last)

print(negate_coords(1, 1, 1))         # unpacked or not, it is one tuple
entries.gotcha: The order in the `return` must match the order in the call; swapping them is one of the three bugs in the week-12 debugging exercise.

entries.title: No return means None; several returns are fine
entries.summary: A function without a `return` hands back `None`. A function may have more than one `return`; the first one reached ends the call.
entries.gotcha: Printing inside a function is not the same as returning. If you want to use the result later, `return` it.

entries.title: Scope: local vs global variables
entries.summary: Variables created inside a function are local and vanish when it returns. Code inside can read outer (global) variables, but assigning inside makes a new local one.
entries.syntax:
z = 2                  # global
def f(x):
    y = x + z          # y is local; z is read from outside
    return y
entries.example:
z = 2                 # global

def show_scope(x):
    y = x + z         # can READ the global z
    return y          # y is LOCAL: it will not exist outside

print(show_scope(6))
print(y)              # NameError: y is local to the function
entries.gotcha: Assigning to a global name inside a function creates a local copy instead (or raises `UnboundLocalError` if you read it first). The `global` keyword changes that, but passing values in and returning them out is cleaner.

entries.title: lambda — a one-line function
entries.summary: A small unnamed function written as `lambda arguments: expression`; the expression's value is returned. Use it for short logic, especially as an argument to `apply`, `sorted` or `map`.
entries.syntax:
lambda x: expression
lambda x, y: expression
f = lambda x: x + 1        # can be named, like any value
entries.example:
add_one = lambda x: x + 1
print(add_one(5))

sum_two = lambda x, y: x + y
print(sum_two(2, 4))

is_non_negative = lambda x: x >= 0
print(is_non_negative(-9), is_non_negative(0))

print((lambda x: x + 1)(5))      # called immediately, without a name

in_range = lambda x, a, b: a <= x <= b
print(in_range(15, 10, 25))
entries.gotcha: No `return` and no statements: a lambda is a single expression. If it needs an `if` with several branches or more than one line, write a `def`.

entries.title: sorted(xs, key=lambda …) — sort by a rule
entries.summary: The `key` argument names a function that computes what to sort by; lambdas shine here.
entries.syntax:
sorted(items, key=lambda x: ...)
sorted(items, key=len, reverse=True)
entries.example:
words = ["python", "R", "julia", "sql"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)))
print(sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True))

scores = {"Ann": 88, "Bob": 95, "Cara": 79}
print(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True))
entries.gotcha: The key function is called on each item and must return something comparable. `sorted` returns a new list and leaves the original alone.

entries.title: List comprehension: [expr for x in xs if cond]
entries.summary: Builds a list in one readable line: an expression for each item, an optional filter. It replaces the build-an-empty-list-then-append pattern.
entries.syntax:
[expression for item in iterable]
[expression for item in iterable if condition]
entries.example:
vals = [1, 5, 6, 8, 12, 15]

print([v % 2 == 1 for v in vals])            # transform: is each one odd?
print([v for v in vals if v % 2 == 0])       # filter: keep the evens
print([v ** 2 for v in vals if v % 2 == 0])  # transform AND filter

stop_words = ["a", "am", "an", "i", "the", "of"]
sentence = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "a", "mat"]
print([w for w in sentence if w not in stop_words])
entries.gotcha: Read it as a sentence: “v squared, for each v in vals, if v is even”. The `if` comes last; an `if … else` that chooses a value goes before the `for` instead.

entries.title: Dict comprehension: {k: v for …}
entries.summary: The same idea for dictionaries: build key–value pairs from an iterable, with an optional filter. Handy for filtering a dict or inverting one.
entries.syntax: {key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable if condition}
entries.gotcha: Keys must be unique: inverting a dict whose values repeat silently keeps only the last pair.

entries.title: str.isdigit() — is this text all digits?
entries.summary: `True` when every character is a digit, which makes it the usual filter for pulling numbers out of a list of strings.
entries.syntax: s.isdigit()
entries.example:
strs = ["99", "red", "16", "balloons"]
print([s.isdigit() for s in strs])
nums = [int(s) for s in strs if s.isdigit()]
print(nums)
print("3.8".isdigit())      # the dot is not a digit
entries.gotcha: `"3.8".isdigit()` and `"-2".isdigit()` are both `False`; the test is for plain whole numbers only.

entries.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
entries.summary: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. It needs a base case, the input for which it stops calling itself.
entries.syntax:
def f(n):
    if n <= 1:            # base case
        return 1
    return n * f(n - 1)   # recursive step on a smaller input
entries.gotcha: Without a base case (or with an input the base case never reaches, such as `fib(-1)`) the calls pile up until `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`. Anything recursive can also be written as a loop.

entries.title: The math and random modules
entries.summary: Two standard-library modules used in the older notebooks: `math` for square roots and rounding down, `random` for a single random number.
entries.syntax:
import math
math.sqrt(x)     math.floor(x)     math.pi

import random
random.seed(n)
random.random()          # a float in [0, 1)
random.randint(a, b)     # an integer in [a, b], both ends included
entries.example:
import math
print(math.sqrt(12))
print(math.floor(2.9), math.floor(2.1))
print(round(math.pi, 4))

import random
random.seed(1)                 # so the numbers repeat
print(random.randint(1, 100))
print(round(random.random(), 3))
entries.gotcha: Unlike NumPy's `randint`, `random.randint(1, 6)` includes 6. For arrays of random numbers use `np.random` instead.

entries.title: class — a blueprint with attributes and methods
entries.summary: A class bundles data (attributes) with functions that act on that data (methods). Every method takes `self` first.
entries.syntax:
class Name:
    """Docstring."""
    attribute = value           # a class attribute

    def method(self):           # a method
        return ...
entries.example:
class Ferrari458:
    """This is a Ferrari 458 object."""
    cylinders = 8                      # a class attribute

    def print_origin(self):            # a method (note: takes self)
        return "I was built in Italy!"

print(Ferrari458.__doc__)
print(type(Ferrari458))
entries.gotcha: Class names are capitalized by convention (`Student`, not `student`). Defining the class builds nothing yet; you still have to create an object from it.

entries.title: Instantiate an object and use the dot operator
entries.summary: Calling the class like a function creates an object (an instance). Reach its attributes and methods with a dot.
entries.syntax:
obj = ClassName()
obj.attribute
obj.method()
entries.example:
class Ferrari458:
    """This is a Ferrari 458 object."""
    cylinders = 8

    def print_origin(self):
        return "I was built in Italy!"

myferrari = Ferrari458()                       # instantiate
print("cylinders:", myferrari.cylinders)       # access an attribute
print("origin   :", myferrari.print_origin())  # call a method
print(type(myferrari).__name__)
entries.output:
cylinders: 8
origin   : I was built in Italy!
Ferrari458
entries.gotcha: Methods are called with parentheses, attributes without: `myferrari.cylinders` but `myferrari.print_origin()`.

entries.title: self — how a method sees its own data
entries.summary: `self` is the object the method was called on. Inside a method, read or set the object's attributes with `self.attribute`.
entries.gotcha: You never pass `self` yourself; Python fills it in when you write `car.get_cylinders()`. Forgetting it in the definition gives `TypeError: get_cylinders() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given`.

entries.title: __init__ — the constructor
entries.summary: `__init__` runs automatically when an object is created, so each object can be given its own values; its parameters can have defaults like any function.
entries.example:
class Ferrari458_v3:
    """This is a Ferrari 458 object."""

    def __init__(self, cylinders, text="I was built in Italy!"):
        self.cylinders = cylinders     # store the passed-in value ON the object
        self.text = text

    def print_origin(self):
        return self.text

ferr1 = Ferrari458_v3(12)
print("cylinders:", ferr1.cylinders)
print("origin   :", ferr1.print_origin())

ferr2 = Ferrari458_v3(10, "I was built in the US!")
print(ferr2.cylinders, "|", ferr2.print_origin())
entries.output:
cylinders: 12
origin   : I was built in Italy!
10 | I was built in the US!
entries.gotcha: Two underscores on each side: `__init__`. Leaving out a required argument raises `TypeError: __init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'cylinders'`.

entries.title: Instances hold independent state
entries.summary: Each object keeps its own attribute values; changing one instance does not touch another.
entries.syntax:
a = Name(1)
b = Name(2)
a.value = 99      # b.value is unchanged
entries.example:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self, start=0):
        self.count = start

    def bump(self):
        self.count += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter(start=10)
a.bump()
a.bump()
b.bump()
print("a:", a.count, "| b:", b.count)
entries.gotcha: A class attribute (defined outside `__init__`) is shared by every instance; attributes set through `self` in `__init__` belong to one object.

entries.title: Never use a mutable default: grades=None, then a fresh list
entries.summary: A default like `grades=[]` is created once and shared by every object, so students would end up sharing one grade list. Default to `None` and make a new list inside.
entries.syntax:
def __init__(self, grades=None):
    self.grades = [] if grades is None else grades
entries.example:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, grades=None):
        self.name = name
        self.grades = [] if grades is None else grades   # a fresh list per student

s1 = Student("Jack")
s2 = Student("Jane")
s1.grades.append(82)
print("s1:", s1.grades, "| s2:", s2.grades)   # s2 is untouched

# the bug, for contrast
class Shared:
    def __init__(self, grades=[]):
        self.grades = grades

a, b = Shared(), Shared()
a.grades.append(82)
print("a:", a.grades, "| b:", b.grades)         # b sees a's grade!
entries.gotcha: The same rule applies to plain functions: never write `def f(items=[])`.

entries.title: A method that updates a list attribute
entries.summary: The Student class from the notebooks: a constructor that stores a list, and a method that appends to it. It is the class you will unit-test the following week.
entries.example:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, id, grades=None):
        self.name = name
        self.id = id
        self.grades = [] if grades is None else grades

    def appendGrade(self, grade):
        self.grades.append(grade)

    def average(self):
        return sum(self.grades) / len(self.grades) if self.grades else 0

s1 = Student("Jack", 123)
s2 = Student("Jane", 456, [90, 95])
s1.appendGrade(82)
s2.appendGrade(80)
print("s1:", s1.grades, "| s2:", s2.grades)
print("s2 average:", round(s2.average(), 2))
entries.gotcha: `average()` guards against an empty list; without the guard, `len(self.grades)` is 0 and the division raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

entries.title: Inheritance: class Child(Parent)
entries.summary: A class can inherit everything from another and add or override behaviour; write the parent in parentheses.
entries.syntax:
class Parent:
    ...

class Child(Parent):      # gets everything from Parent
    def method(self):     # ...and may override a method
        ...
entries.gotcha: The child reuses the parent's `__init__` unless it defines its own. This is how libraries specialize types (`unittest.TestCase` is a parent you inherit from in week 11).

entries.title: Common exceptions and how to read a traceback
entries.summary: When Python cannot run a line it raises an exception and stops. The last line of the red traceback names the type and the reason; that line is the one to read first.
entries.syntax:
ZeroDivisionError   dividing by 0
NameError           using a name that does not exist
IndexError          list position out of range
KeyError            missing dict key
TypeError           wrong type for an operation ("a" + 1)
ValueError          right type, bad value (int("abc"))
FileNotFoundError   opening a file that is not there
entries.example:
examples = [
    lambda: 3 / 0,
    lambda: undefined_var,
    lambda: [10, 20, 30][5],
    lambda: {"a": 1}["b"],
    lambda: "a" + 1,
    lambda: int("abc"),
    lambda: open("missing.txt"),
]
for run in examples:
    try:
        run()
    except Exception as e:          # show each error instead of stopping at the first
        print(type(e).__name__, "->", e)
entries.output:
ZeroDivisionError -> division by zero
NameError -> name 'undefined_var' is not defined
IndexError -> list index out of range
KeyError -> 'b'
TypeError -> can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
ValueError -> invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
FileNotFoundError -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'
entries.gotcha: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the last line says what went wrong, the lines above it say where. The arrow points at the line in your own code.

entries.title: try / except — handle an error instead of crashing
entries.summary: Wrap risky code in `try`; if it raises the named exception, the `except` block runs and the program continues.
entries.gotcha: Name the exception you expect (`except ValueError:`). A bare `except:` swallows every error, including your own typos, and hides bugs.

entries.title: else and finally
entries.summary: `else` runs only when the `try` block raised nothing; `finally` runs no matter what, which makes it the place for cleanup.
entries.output:
division succeeded
  (finally: this always runs)
10/2 -> 5.0
  cannot divide by zero — returning None
  (finally: this always runs)
10/0 -> None
entries.gotcha: `finally` runs even after a `return` inside `try` or `except`, which is exactly what makes it reliable for closing files and connections.

entries.title: except SomeError as e — keep the message
entries.summary: `as e` binds the exception object so you can print its message or inspect its type.
entries.syntax:
except ValueError as e:
    print("caught:", e)
entries.output:
caught: age cannot be negative, got -5
type  : ValueError
entries.gotcha: The name `e` only exists inside the `except` block.

entries.title: raise — fail loudly with your own message
entries.summary: `raise` throws an exception on purpose, so bad input is rejected early with a clear message instead of producing a wrong answer later.
entries.syntax:
if condition_is_bad:
    raise ValueError("what went wrong and what was received")
entries.output:
21
ValueError: age cannot be negative, got -5
entries.gotcha: Pick the exception type that fits: `ValueError` for a bad value, `TypeError` for a wrong type. A raised error is meant to be caught by the caller with `try`/`except`.

entries.title: assert condition, message
entries.summary: Does nothing when the condition is `True`; raises `AssertionError` with your message when it is `False`. A quick sanity check while developing.
entries.syntax: assert condition, "message shown if it fails"
entries.example:
def average(values):
    assert len(values) > 0, "cannot average an empty list"
    return sum(values) / len(values)

print(average([90, 95, 80]))

num_args = 3
assert num_args == 3, "number of arguments must be 3!"
print("first check passed")

print(average([]))
entries.output:
88.33333333333333
first check passed
AssertionError: cannot average an empty list
entries.gotcha: Use `assert` to check assumptions during development; use `raise` for input validation that must always run.

entries.title: A quick assertEqual with unittest.TestCase()
entries.summary: The fastest taste of unit testing: make a `TestCase` object and call its assert methods directly. A passing check returns `None`; a failing one raises `AssertionError`.
entries.syntax:
import unittest
tc = unittest.TestCase()
tc.assertEqual(actual, expected)
entries.example:
import unittest

tc = unittest.TestCase()

actual = 10 % 2 == 0
print(tc.assertEqual(actual, True))      # passes: returns None
print("first assertion passed")

try:
    tc.assertEqual(10 % 2 == 1, True)    # fails
except AssertionError as e:
    print("second assertion failed:", e)
entries.output:
None
first assertion passed
second assertion failed: False != True
entries.gotcha: Put the value your code produced first and the expected value second; the failure message reads `actual != expected`.

entries.title: A TestCase subclass with test_ methods
entries.summary: The real way: inherit from `unittest.TestCase`, write one method per behaviour, each named `test_...`, and assert inside it. Test-driven development writes these before the code.
entries.output:
test_append_adds_a_grade (__main__.TestStudent.test_append_adds_a_grade) ... ok
test_new_student_has_no_grades (__main__.TestStudent.test_new_student_has_no_grades) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 2 tests in 0.000s

OK
passed: True
entries.gotcha: Method names must start with `test_` or the runner ignores them. Tests run in alphabetical order, not the order you wrote them; number them (`test_1_...`) if order matters.

entries.title: Run tests inside a notebook
entries.summary: In Colab or Jupyter, load the tests from the class and hand them to a runner; or call `unittest.main` with the arguments that keep it from exiting the kernel.
entries.syntax:
suite = unittest.TestLoader().loadTestsFromTestCase(TestStudent)
unittest.TextTestRunner(verbosity=2).run(suite)

# alternative, runs every TestCase in the notebook
_ = unittest.main(argv=["first-arg-is-ignored"], exit=False)
entries.gotcha: A plain `unittest.main()` in a notebook tries to exit the kernel (`SystemExit`); the `argv=..., exit=False` form is the notebook-safe one.

entries.title: unittest.main() in a script
entries.summary: In a `.py` file, the standard ending: `unittest.main()` under the `__main__` guard, so `python test_student.py` runs every test.
entries.syntax:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
entries.setup_note: write test_student.py (a %%writefile cell in Colab, or any editor locally)
entries.example: !python test_student.py
entries.gotcha: Test output goes to the error stream, which is why it looks red in Colab even when everything passed. `OK` at the end is the verdict.

entries.title: assertEqual, assertTrue, assertIn, assertRaises …
entries.summary: `TestCase` provides a family of checks; each accepts an optional message shown when it fails.
entries.syntax:
assertEqual(a, b)          a == b
assertNotEqual(a, b)       a != b
assertTrue(x)              bool(x) is True
assertFalse(x)             bool(x) is False
assertIn(a, b)             a in b
assertIsNone(x)            x is None
assertIsInstance(a, B)     isinstance(a, B)
with self.assertRaises(Err): ...    the block raises Err
entries.example:
import unittest

class TestExamples(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_asserts(self):
        self.assertEqual(2 + 2, 4)
        self.assertNotEqual("a", "b")
        self.assertTrue("x" in "xyz")
        self.assertIn(3, [1, 2, 3])
        self.assertIsNone(None)
        self.assertIsInstance(3.5, float)
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            int("abc")

_ = unittest.main(argv=["first-arg-is-ignored"], exit=False)
entries.gotcha: If a test can fail in more than one way, split it into separate tests, and use the `msg` argument to say what went wrong.

entries.title: if __name__ == "__main__":
entries.summary: When a file runs directly, Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"`; when it is imported, `__name__` is the module's name. The guard lets a file offer reusable functions and a runnable demo.
entries.example:
!python moduleX.py          # run directly -> the __main__ block executes

import moduleX              # import -> functions available, demo does NOT run
print("imported OK:", moduleX.function1())
print(moduleX.__name__)
entries.output:
running moduleX directly:
inside function1
inside function2
imported OK: inside function1
moduleX
entries.gotcha: Without the guard, `import moduleX` would run the demo code too, which is rarely what you want.

entries.title: %%writefile — save a cell as a .py file
entries.summary: A cell magic: the first line names the file and the rest of the cell is written to it, so a notebook can create real scripts.
entries.syntax:
%%writefile script.py
code...
entries.example:
%%writefile hello.py
print("Hello from a script")
entries.gotcha: `%%writefile` must be the very first line of the cell, alone. The cell writes the file but does not run it; run it with `!python hello.py`.

entries.title: Run a script: !python script.py in Colab, python script.py in a terminal
entries.summary: Outside notebooks, Python lives in `.py` files run from the command line. In Colab the same command works with a `!` in front.
entries.syntax:
!python script.py         # Colab cell
python script.py          # terminal
entries.setup:
%%writefile hello.py
print("Hello from a script")
print(2 + 2)
entries.example: !python hello.py
entries.gotcha: `python: can't open file 'hello.py'` means the file is not in the current folder. Check with `!ls` (Colab) or `ls` (terminal).

entries.title: Import your own file as a module
entries.summary: Any `.py` file in the working folder can be imported by its name (without `.py`); its functions are then available with a dot.
entries.syntax:
import moduleX
moduleX.function1()
entries.example:
import stats_helpers

scores = [88, 92, 79]
print(stats_helpers.mean(scores))
print(stats_helpers.spread(scores))
entries.gotcha: Python imports a module once per session; after editing the file, restart the runtime (or use `importlib.reload`) to pick up the changes.

entries.title: sys.argv — command-line arguments
entries.summary: `sys.argv` is the list of words typed after `python` on the command line; `argv[0]` is the script name and the rest are your arguments, always as strings.
entries.syntax:
import sys
n = int(sys.argv[1])      # convert: arguments arrive as text
entries.setup_note: write fibonacci_arg.py, a script that reads n from the command line
entries.example:
!python fibonacci_arg.py 6
!python fibonacci_arg.py 10
entries.gotcha: Forgetting the `int()` makes `fibonacci("6")` compare text with numbers and fail; the assignment hint “what is the data type of the argument?” points here.

entries.title: hasattr() — verify that a method exists
entries.summary: AI assistants sometimes invent methods. `hasattr(obj, "name")` checks in one line whether the object really has it.
entries.syntax: hasattr(obj, "method_name")
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
print(hasattr(df, "average"))    # False: the method was hallucinated
print(hasattr(df, "mean"))       # True: this one is real
print(df["x"].mean())            # verify the correct call yourself
entries.gotcha: Trust, but verify: read AI-suggested code, run it on a small example, and unit-test it. A confident answer is not a correct one.

entries.title: Debugging pattern: define a function before you call it
entries.summary: Bug 1 of the in-class debugging activity: the function is called on a line above its `def`. Python reads top to bottom, so the name does not exist yet.
entries.syntax:
# wrong order
result = summarize(df)
def summarize(df): ...

# right order
def summarize(df): ...
result = summarize(df)
entries.gotcha: In a notebook the same error appears when the cell with the `def` has not been run yet in this session.

entries.title: Debugging pattern: match the return order to the call
entries.summary: Bug 2 of the debugging activity: the function returns `season_stats, size_counts` but the call unpacks `size_counts, season_stats`. No error is raised; the names simply hold the wrong tables.
entries.example:
def summarize(values):
    small = [v for v in values if v < 10]
    large = [v for v in values if v >= 10]
    return small, large            # small first, large second

small, large = summarize([3, 12, 7, 25])     # matches the return order
print("small:", small, "| large:", large)

large, small = summarize([3, 12, 7, 25])     # swapped: runs, but the names lie
print("small:", small, "| large:", large)
entries.gotcha: Silent bugs are the dangerous kind. After unpacking, print each name once to confirm it holds what you think.

entries.title: .str.capitalize() and .map(dict) on a column
entries.summary: Two column tools from the debugging activity's fix: `.str.capitalize()` normalizes text case, and `.map(dictionary)` translates each value through a lookup table.
entries.syntax:
df["col"].str.capitalize()
df["col"].map({"jan": "Winter", ...})
entries.example:
import pandas as pd

fire = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["mar", "oct", "aug", "feb"]})
season_map = {"Dec": "Winter", "Jan": "Winter", "Feb": "Winter",
              "Mar": "Spring", "Apr": "Spring", "May": "Spring",
              "Jun": "Summer", "Jul": "Summer", "Aug": "Summer",
              "Sep": "Fall",   "Oct": "Fall",   "Nov": "Fall"}

fire["season"] = fire["month"].str.capitalize().map(season_map)
print(fire)
entries.output:
month  season
0   mar  Spring
1   oct    Fall
2   aug  Summer
3   feb  Winter
entries.gotcha: `.map` returns `NaN` for values missing from the dictionary, so a lowercase `"mar"` against capitalized keys gives all `NaN`; normalize the case first.

entries.title: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt (and %matplotlib inline)
entries.summary: `pyplot`, aliased `plt`, is the base layer almost every Python plot sits on. The `%matplotlib inline` magic makes figures appear under the cell in older notebooks; Colab does this by default.
entries.syntax:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
%matplotlib inline      # optional in Colab
entries.example:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib
print(matplotlib.__version__)
print(type(plt.figure()).__name__)
entries.gotcha: The magic line starts with `%` and must be on its own line. It is not Python, so it fails in a `.py` script.

entries.title: !pip install -q plotnine — install a package in Colab
entries.summary: Colab has most libraries preinstalled; for the rest, a `!pip install` line in a cell adds them to the session.
entries.syntax: !pip install -q package_name
entries.example:
!pip install -q plotnine
import plotnine
print("plotnine", plotnine.__version__)
entries.gotcha: Installs are forgotten when the runtime ends; keep the line in the Setup cell so it runs every time. `!pip` is fine in Colab because it has only one Python; in a terminal on your own computer write `python -m pip install …` so that pip belongs to the Python you are running (see `shell/pip-install`), and in a local notebook `%pip install …` is the equivalent safeguard.

entries.title: plt.plot — the basic plot, with format strings
entries.summary: Draws y against x. A short format string sets the marker, line and color: `'o'` circles with no line, `'.-r'` red dots joined by a line.
entries.syntax:
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.plot(x, y, 'o')                     # circle markers, no line
plt.plot(x, y, '.-r')                   # red dots with a line
plt.plot(x, y, color='steelblue', marker='o', linestyle='', markersize=4)
entries.setup:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)
entries.example:
plt.plot(iris["sepal_length"], iris["sepal_width"], 'o', color='steelblue', markersize=4)
plt.title("Sepal width vs. length")
plt.xlabel("sepal length (cm)")
plt.ylabel("sepal width (cm)")
plt.show()
entries.gotcha: Without a format string `plt.plot` joins the points with a line in data order, which turns a scatter into spaghetti. Use `'o'` or `plt.scatter` for points.

entries.title: plt.title, xlabel, ylabel, show
entries.summary: The recipe for every matplotlib chart: draw, then label the title and both axes, then `plt.show()`.
entries.syntax:
plt.title("...")
plt.xlabel("...")
plt.ylabel("...")
plt.show()
entries.setup: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
entries.example:
years = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026]
enrollment = [24, 27, 31, 30, 35]

plt.plot(years, enrollment, '.-')
plt.title("HUDM 5001 enrollment")
plt.xlabel("year")
plt.ylabel("students")
plt.show()
entries.gotcha: Label everything: a chart without axis labels tells your reader nothing about units. `plt.show()` ends the figure; calls after it start a new one.

entries.title: plt.style.use — change the whole look
entries.summary: One line switches the theme of every chart that follows; `'ggplot'` mimics R, `'default'` resets.
entries.syntax:
plt.style.available            # the list
plt.style.use('ggplot')
plt.style.use('default')

 + geom_histogram(aes(x='sepal_length', fill='species'), bins=20)
 + theme_minimal()
 + labs(title='Sepal length by species'))
entries.gotcha: Leave out `bins` and plotnine warns you to pick a better value. Pick one on purpose.

entries.title: geom_boxplot — x is the group, y the value
entries.summary: One box per category with the mapping given once, in `ggplot(...)`, so every later layer shares it.
entries.syntax: ggplot(df, aes(x='group', y='value')) + geom_boxplot()
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, geom_boxplot, theme_minimal, labs

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)
entries.example:
(ggplot(iris, aes(x='species', y='sepal_length'))
 + geom_boxplot()
 + theme_minimal()
 + labs(title='Sepal length by species'))
entries.gotcha: Aesthetics given in `ggplot()` apply to all layers; aesthetics given inside a `geom_*()` apply to that layer only.

entries.title: geom_point with color=
entries.summary: A scatter plot; mapping `color` to a category draws each group in its own color with a legend for free.
entries.syntax: ggplot(df, aes(x='a', y='b', color='group')) + geom_point()
entries.setup:

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)
entries.example:
(ggplot(iris, aes(x='petal_length', y='petal_width', color='species'))
 + geom_point()
 + theme_minimal()
 + labs(title='Petal width vs length by species'))
entries.gotcha: `color` inside `aes()` maps a column; `geom_point(color='red')` outside `aes()` sets one fixed color.

entries.title: facet_wrap — small multiples
entries.summary: Splits one plot into a panel per value of a variable, the superpower for comparing groups on identical axes.
entries.syntax: ... + facet_wrap('group')
entries.setup:
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, geom_point, facet_wrap, theme_minimal, labs

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"
iris = pd.read_csv(IRIS_URL)

(ggplot(iris, aes(x='sepal_width', y='sepal_length', color='species'))
 + geom_point()
 + facet_wrap('species')           # one panel per species
 + theme_minimal()
 + labs(title='Sepal length vs width, faceted by species'))
entries.gotcha: Panels share the same axes by default, which is what makes them comparable; do not “fix” that unless the scales really differ.

entries.title: theme_minimal() and labs()
entries.summary: `theme_minimal()` gives a clean look; `labs()` sets the title and axis labels in one call.
entries.syntax: ... + theme_minimal() + labs(title='...', x='...', y='...')

entries.title: px.scatter — an interactive scatter plot
entries.summary: Plotly Express makes charts you can hover, zoom and pan; `color=` splits by group and `hover_data` adds columns to the tooltip. Show a figure with `fig.show()`.
entries.syntax:
import plotly.express as px
fig = px.scatter(df, x='a', y='b', color='group', title='...', hover_data=['c'])
fig.show()

entries.title: px.histogram with barmode='overlay'
entries.summary: An interactive histogram; `color=` gives one series per group and `barmode='overlay'` draws them on top of each other instead of stacked.
entries.syntax: px.histogram(df, x='value', color='group', barmode='overlay').show()

entries.title: px.bar — an interactive bar chart
entries.summary: Bars from a summary table: give the category column as `x` and the height column as `y`.

import plotly.express as px

IRIS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cgpan/hudm5001/main/asset/iris.csv"

entries.title: Which chart for which question
entries.summary: Match the chart to the question, label everything, and save the figure for your report.
entries.syntax:
How is one numeric variable distributed?        histogram / density
How do groups compare on a numeric variable?   boxplot / violin
How do two numeric variables relate?            scatter
How big is each category?                       bar
How does something change over time?            line
entries.gotcha: The same question has one chart in each library: histogram is `plt.hist`, `geom_histogram`, `px.histogram`. Learn the question first, then the syntax.
